TWO NEW YEAR SONGS. Who comes dancing over the snow, His little soft feet all bare and rosy? Open the door though the wild winds blow; Take the child in and make him cosy. Take him in, and hold him dear; He is the wonderful New Year. Open your heart, be it sad or gay, ' Welcome him there and use him kindly; For you must carry him, yea or nay-, Carry him with shut eyes so blindly. But whether he bringeth joy or fear, Take him! God sends him—this good New Year.

A small ship launched upon an unknown sea, A small seed planted from an unknown tree, Such is this strange New Year to you and me. Whither the vessel goeth, And how the tree upgroweth, God only k-noweth. But sail the ship and plant the seed, What's done in faith is done in deed. the Author of" John Halifax, Gentleman." THE OLD YEAR AND THE NEW. How swift they go, Life's many years, With their winds of woe And their storms of tears, And the darkest of nights whose shadowy slopes Are lit with the flashes of starriest hopes, And their sunshiny days on whose calm heavens loom The clouds of the tempest—the shadows of gloom! And ah ! we pray With a grief so drear, That the years may stay When their graves are near; Tho' the brows of to-morrows be radiant and bright, With love and with beauty, with life and with light, The dead hearts of yesterdays, cold on the bier, To the hearts that survive them are evermore dear.
For the heart so true To each Ord Year rieaves ; Tho' the hand of tho New

Flowory garlands weaves. • But the lowers of the future, though fragrant and fair, With the past's withered leaflets may never compare; For dear is each dead leaf—and dearer each thorn— In the wreaths which the brows of our past years have worn;

Tea! mem will cling With a love to the last, - And mildly fling Their arms round the past! As the vine that clings to the oak that falls, As the ivy twines round the tumbling walls, For the dint of the past some hearts higher pine, Than the stars that Rash mit from the futtne's skies.

And why nat so? The old, ata years, They knew and they know AA our .hapes and fears; .• We wafked try their side, and we bold them each grief, Aiad they kissed off our tears whila they whispered relief; And the stories of hearts that may not be ;revealed In the hearts of the dead years are buried and sealed.

Let the Now Year sing At the Old Yeses grave; Will the 14ew Year bring What the Old Year gave? h! the'Strangm. Year trips over the SLOWS, And tis brow is wreathed with many n rose; But how many thorns LA) the roses conceal Which the roses, whenavithered, shalbso soon reveal?

Let the New T;ear smite While the OH Year dies; ori.„B4P-- In how-short a while Shall the smiles be aighs ? .71 'Teal Stranger Tear, tiou hest many a charm, Andfliy face is fair acd thy-greeting warm, But nearer than thou—in h shroud of snows-- Is the furrowed faceef the Wear that goes. Tea! .hright New Year, O'er alrtW earth, With gangland cheer. They wilt liail thy birth; They will trust thy wordsiin a single hour, thylace, they Wilt 'laud thy power, ‘JWor the New has charms adhichthe Old has not, 41 Andithe StrangertsEace makes' tLe Friend's' forgot. JOIST,/ GRE/EiTEAV Warn-MR.—Probably no Ming man in the Thritedfltates has more -of the admiration, love, and reverence of his countrymen. He has fortunately illustrated an agreement 'of many paradoxes. With a frail physical -constitution, and with life-long ailments, he has attained to great age; with the scantiest outfit of esatlyaeducationhe has become a well-read man and skil- ful and influential writer; reamed among farmers in a lonely neighbourhood, he had from the beginning the simple and distinguished manners which belong to 'the 'highest society:: a chivalrous admirer of women, he has remained unmarried; without inherited wealth, he has 'maintained theastate-of a gentleman; a devotee to the principles of peace, ke has been most active in the 'movement which led to the "great Civil War; 'once the unsparing denunciator of the orthodox clergy and the great political 'leaders for subservience to elavery, he has lived te win their respect and hosnage ; a member .of a sect which has lightly valued the graces and has pat poetry and song under ban, he has lived in an ideal world of beauty and melody, and shown him- self the most truly spontaneous and inspired of poets; the most ebstemious and self-controlled of men, his verse often exhibits many glowing traits that remind us of the 'brilliant and passion-blinded Burns; brought up far from the centre of academic influence, he has be- come a member of that higher •circle of great minds for whom worally honours and scholastic titles are useless and belittling.—F. UNWERWOOD, in Good Words for January. LORD SITAFTESBER'T AND THE Coseras.—One resuit of the excitement of that time was the establishment of s‘ The London Union of Geseral Dealers." The meetings are 'held in the Golden Lane Mission Roam, and every- thing touching the general welfare of the costerinonQer fraternity is there discussed. At one of the meetings, -when the threatened evil was under dismission, Lord' Shaftesbury told the men that at any time, when they had grievances which he could assist them to get re- dressed, they should write to him, and he would not fail to respond. "But where shall we write to ?" asked one of them.'" Address your letter to me at Grosv4nor Square, and it will probably reach -isse," he replied: 4` but if after my name you put ' ICH. and Coster,' there will be no doubt that I shall get it" One of the strangest ceremonials that ever took place at a public meeting occurred in 1875, in connection with this society. Lord Shaftesbury, who was president of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, had taken a deep Interest in the costermongeru' donkeys. It was pro- verbial, at one time, that both the donkeys and ponies were shamefully ill-used; but by education and exhorta- tation, by the institution of donkey shows a.nd prizes, and a variety of other means, the men of Golden Lane had come to take a pride in their animals, and had found that kind and just treatment was the wisest policy. With twenty-four hours' rest on Sunday, they would do thirty miles a day without exhaustion; whereas, without it, they did not do an average of more than fifteen. In recognition of his kind services, the costers invited Lord Shaftesbury to meet them in their Hall to receive a presentation. Over a thousand casters, with their friends, were there, and the platform was graced by many ladies and gentlemen, when 'a handsome donkey, profusely decorated with ribands, "was led on to the platform and presented as a token of esteem to the ehairrnan. Lord Shaftesbury good-humouredly vacated the chair and made way for the new arrival, and then, putting his arm round the animal's neck returned thanks in a short speech, in which, however, there was a ring of pathos, as he said, "When I have passed away from this life, I desire to have no more said of me than that I have done my duty, as the poor donkey has done his, with patience and unmurmuring resignation." The donkey was then led down the steps of the platform, and Lard Shaftesbury remarked, "I hope the reporters of the Press will state that, the donkey having vacated the chair, the place was taken bv Lord Shaftesbeay.e_ Life and firor7c of the Seventh Zarl of Shaftesbury, by E(lzoln Hodder _Tr'nFh. red, or chapped skin there is nothing equal to tnams Glycerine and Cucumber." The silent pressure of the hand 'is often of more Vital good than a whole volume of counsel; and one tear, one kiss,fcne bright encouraging smile, can help the broken heart, the sinking spirit, where words of advice would fall unheeded, or be an aggravation to present pain. Care is something that rightly falls to the lot of all. Childhood alone may claim exemption from it. As the life advances, it comes with every new responsibility, anti every' honest man and woman accepts it cheerfully as his or her share in the world's burdens. So far, how- ever, care is ne grinding taSkmaster. It develops power, it encourages endeavour, It promotes happiness. No one but the selfish idler would wish to be entirely 'free from care; but we justly hold him in honour who 'faithfully ' takes up that which falls to bialot, and fulfils the duties it involves. OVER THE RANGE IN STYLE.—It may be gathered from the following, taken from an American contemporary, that histrionics "out West" are not unaccompanied by a criticism of details somewhat embarrassing to the average-strolling player---" The sun was shining brightly on Union-square when Harold Montgomery Boothbarrett - strode into the centre of a group of actors. Why, Harold,' said one, I thought you had gone out West with a company to play Shakesperian plays! You have cut your trip short, havn't you ? " Young man, I under- took to play Romeo and Juliet in Butte City, Montana. All went merry as a marriage bell till I was about to stab myself in the last act. When I drew the dagger, the audience-burst into a roar of laughter, and a rude fellow in the front row called out "Hey, you 'tender-foot, wat are you-goin' ter do P" I was astonished; but I replied, "To kill myself." '"Wot," said he," with that tooth- pick? You can't come that on this ,community. You take this and send yourself over the range in style ; " and he handed me-up a tremendous 'revolver. I expos- \tulated, and explained that it was not in the play. I said they had no pistols in those days. Wet!" he roared. "No pistols? Then the quicker you stop this play an' give us a song an' dance the better? And Juliet and I had to do the "Big Sunflower" right there, dressed just as we were. Young man, Shakespere's get no show out there !' " A MAD ENGINE Minim—A Son's TALE.—I was beginning to get alarmed; and looking out over the well-known country—for I had travelled that journey many and many a time before--d saw that we were much nearer to Blinton than we ought to be at that hour. However, I thought it did not much matter, for the line was signalled clear in front of us, and the damage done was, as yet, simply a little waste of coal. In a few minutes, our speed increased enormously, and ' I calculated we were travelling at the rate of seventy miles an hour. thought it was time to remonstrate; and turning to Morgan, I noticed that the indicator showed full speed. I called his attention to the fact, and begged him to reduce‘the speed, or we should run into Blinton without being able to stop. '4‘ Ha, ha!" he cried in reply. "Stop"! I'm never going to stop again! I told .you I'd make *her traveL What do you want to stop for 2—Get on -old wench, get on'f" Then he burst into a hideous pdl of laughter. A -cold -sweat of absolute terror broke out on me as I realised the state of things. Here was a raving maniac, a far stronger man than myself, in charge of a train full of people. I bit my lips and clenched my hands, and tried-to collect my scattered ideas and decide what was beetle, be don; Meanwhile, Morgnn sat on a rail near the boiler flourishing a shovel and shouting-uproariously. The-train rushed on with incredible speed, not steadily and evenly, but with leaps and bounds, that threatened to ,east the engine off the line at every yard. There was no doubt the man was as mad as a man -could be, and he was also master of the situation. I made one effort to reach the handle by which the steam is turned off; but the madman was too sharp for me. "No, you don't?" he shouted. He brought his shovel down with a tremendous blow on the rail at my side,Just missing mytead. It was plain I could do nothing by force. Would stratagem be of any use? I looked out to the country; time was running short; we were not more than twenty miles from Blinton Junction; and if we did not atop there, the whole train must inevitably be wrecked, and probably not one passenger would escape uninjured, and but few with their lives. I looked back to ;the train. Outside the windows were hands gesticulating, and frightened, alarmed faces. At the end of the train, the guard was waving a red flag. Something must be done, and by me, or we should all 'be inevitably lost. I made up my mind. I turned to Morgan with a smile on my face, and I said: "Old bon-youlre quite right-; this is a fine pace; but it ain't quite 'fast enough. 'Leek here?' and I caught him by the arm and led 'him to the side of the engine next to the double rail. "See'!" I cried ; " there is another train coming up faster than us, and she will pass us; we must go faster; but let's see first who is driving her; lean forward and look. Can you see?" The poor maniac stepped outside the rail and leaned forward to look for the imaginary train, when I gave him a sudden push, and he fell in a- heap on the side rails and was killed on the spot. With% gasp of relief I sprang back to the engine and turned eff the steam. It was not a moment too soon. We were well in sight of Blinton Junction before I had the train properly under control. I pulled up at the platform all right, and then I fainted. When I came to, I was lying on a bench in , the waiting-room and the inspector was standing over me, with his note-book in his hand, prepared to take , down my statement. What I stated was that the engine- driver had gone mad, and that, t,q save the lives of the passengers, I had knocked him off the engine just in time to get the train under ;control before running into the station. This was corroborated by the guard and several passengers; and the case was brought before the solici- tors of the company. I gave my evidence at the inquest, and heard no more of the matter until onelday the passenger superintendent handed me ten-sovereigns and a letter appointing me station-master of Little Isludford. It was evident the directors condoned my conduct; and I hope that my readers will agree with them, and, in consideration of my having saved a train full of people, will acquit me of murder, ;and bring in a verdict of justifiable homicide.--Chandiers's Joe, mat.

OUSTING THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.

Dr. O'Keeffe moved that the recommendation previously passed respecting applying to the Local Government Board for one-half of the salary of the medical .officer and sanitary inspector be rescinded. The committee. Dr. O'Keeffe said, considered it was better that both medizal officer and sani- tary inspector should be entirely under the control of the Local Board. They found that if they gave the Local Go- vernment Board an inch they took an ell.—Mr. Heves seconded, and remarked that the Local Government Beard had shown a strong desire to interfere.—Mr. Husband said the Local Government Board also insisted upon their adver- tising for medical officer and inspector, which would be unfair to other persons who might apply, as they had no fault te find with their present officers.—The motion .was then carried, and the Board went into Committee on ether business.

THE BIRKENHEAD ExpLostotr.—The inquest on the bodies of the ten men who lost their lives on Sunday., the 2Cth ult., by an explosion on board the steamship Petriana, at Birkenhead, concluded on Wednesday. The jury con- sidered it absolutely necessarr that, is carrying on work on board petroleum ships, the electric light or safety lamps only should be used. Two LivEnosTs SWANPED.--LOSS 4OF TWENTY LIVES.— intelligence has been received from F.'srfolk,Virginia, of the wreck of the ship Elizabeth. bound from Hamburg for Baltimore. The vessel was driven ashore near Cape Henry, at the entrance of Chesapeake Bac, during a gale, accom- panied by a blinding snowstorm. Two lifeboats went to her assistance, and succeeded in taking off the crew, which numbered 15 men, but an enormous wave swamped both boats. The whole of the ship's crew, as well as five of the rescuers, were drowned. The Elizabeth is expected to be- come a total wreck.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board Offices, on Tuesday afternoon. There wero present—Messrs Gossage (chairman), E. Carey, D. Wright, R. Cook, F. Heves. J. Taylor, H. Gaskell, jun., S. Sadler, T. Handley, W. W. Gossage, B. Brown, Dr. O'Keeffe, Midwood, W. T. Husband ; J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higginson (surveyor), I. Carr (gas engineer), J. Dickson (inspector).

div.head: AN ANONYMOUS BATEPAVER.
div.p: AN ANONYMOUS BATEPAVER.

The Clerk read a letter he had received, signed "Rate- payer." The writer stated that he had seen lamplighters working for private persons, and be remarked that be did not like to see this when there were so many workmen out et employment. He thought if lamplighters had so much time to spare they should work in the yard.—The Chairman thought a gentleman who wrote such a letter as that ought to put his name to it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Gaskell said the Board simply paid the lamplighters for lightiug and ex- tinguishing the lamps, and they had nothing further to do with them or with the way in which they spent the rest of their time. It was to the advantage cf the ratepayers that the lamplighters should be free to get other occupations, for in that case the Board got them at a cheaper rate.—The matter then dropped.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMICTTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMICTTEE.

The minutes of this committee stated that the engineer's report contained the following :—The rainfall for the month had been—Gas yard gnage 4 094 inches, Pea Hill guage 4.180 iaches, mean 4.137 inches. Water in stock December 29th, 1886, 11,309,443 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month has averaged 18.28 candles. The wages required during the next four weeks is for gas and waterworks £95 per week. Stock's well: Foundations of No. 2 engine house. The working of making good these foundations is now fairly forward, about 65 tonsaf concrete has been put in as shown on accompanying itlan. Bore Hole, No. 2 Well : Mr. Timmins's men commenced clearing 'this bore hole on the 20th ult., which was found to contain 39 feet of sand mixed with pieces of timber and bricks, bolts, washers, nuts, dm. 27 feet has been got oat, and the remainder will I expect be cleared in a few days. Burst Pipe: On Sunday morning the 26th ult., the 14. inch water main in Hutchinson-street burst, the metal of the pipe was, las in previous instances, found to be greatly decemposed by the action of the slag and cinders of which the ground is composed. Sulphate Plant: This-plant worked 20 days last month; ten tons have been sold; present stock 12 tons. Fire Brigade: I would recommend that some additional boss be purchased for the use of the 'fire brigade, at the recent fire at Messrs. Mathieson's ; what we bad was very insuffi- cient. If a hand hose-reel cart was provided it would be of great service for running the hose out in narrow passages and places about the various works and railw.ay sidings where it is impossible to get the engine. Fire Brigade: Recommended, that a hand reel and 300 feet of hose pipe, estimated to cost £BO, be purchased. Illegal use of Water: The engineer reported that a tap in W. Streets' yard, Alforde-street, had been left open on 23rd December, thereby causing a great waste of water. Recommended, that Wm. Streets be prosecuted. Letter, 15th December, from J. Muspratt and Sons, stating precautions have been taken to prevent water being taken from their stablee. Public Lamps: The engineer reported that John McCririe, No. 30, Mill-brow, had wilfully broken one of the street lamps, on 20th December. Recommended, that John McCririe be prosecuted. Coke: Recommended, that the contract with S. Kidd for 5 tone per week over 1887, at 7s per ton Lox, less 2i per cent., be approved. Recommended that the price of coke be reduced to fourpence per cwt. until further notice.—Mr. Gasket( moved, and Mr. Sadler seconded, the adoption of the minutes.-111r. Carey, referring to the burst- in.( of the main in klutchinson•street, asked if the pipes were now being laid In puddle, or some such suitable mate- rial, so that cinders would not get against them in future.— Mr. Gaskeli said that all new pipes were being laid in pud- dle, and they were gradually replacing those that had been laid in cinders.—The minutes were coefirmed. :1;21.1,4

div.head: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.

The Highway Committee's minutes contained as follows: —Main Sewer: Recommended that a 15-inch pipe sewer be placed in Anne-street, from junction of Caroline-street to Lugsdale-road. Plans approved for sewer from Anderson's Corner to Oxford-street, Lugs.lale-road, and from the Vine- yard Crossing to East-street, Warrington-road. Wages es- timated for the next four weeks, £37 lOs per week. The Surveyor's report readt—Steam Roller: The steam roller has been engaged rolling various roads in the townships. Private Street Improvements: The contractors are still en- gaged carrying out their contracts in the various streets. Anne Street : The completing of the repairs in this street is delayed in consequence of not being able to get the stone from Mr. Newsome. Brynn Street Sewering: Messrs. Sayce and Randle have nearly completed this work. Footpath to Moss Bank I have examined the footpath and it is in good repair. Public Lighting: Four of Bray's lanterns have been fixed on the old columns in Victoria-road. The lamp ordered to be fixed in Lugsdalc-lane has not yet been done owing to the Gas Committee's men being otherwise en- gaged. Re-numbering: The following streets have been re-numbered: Charlotte-street, Caroline-street, Margaret- street, Oxford-street, Victoria-street, Vine-street, Violet- street, Dickson-street, Pool-street, Wareing-street, Major- Cross-street, and Sutton's-lane. ROBBERY Orli, ,K CHEST. century ago there resided in the -hood of _.:ley an eccentric personage. who , 'amiliarly known as "Johnny Steele." The neighbours were well aware that Johnny was rich, he having inherited considerable wealth from his parents, who were of very parsimonious habits. His miserly propensities prevented him from.depositing his cash in a bank, which, he said, might break at any moment, and a similar fear also prevented him from investing in any kind of securities, or even of employing his capital in any kind of trade or profitable business. He followed with contentment the simple life of a small farmer, and hoarded up his accumulated wealth in an old oaken chest in his own domicile, wrapping the chest round in all directions with massive iron chains, secured by means of padlocks and other fastenings. The fact that Johnny had such a rich hoard was known far and near, and he was often warned, some- times in joke and sometimes in earnest, of the risk he ran in keeping his money in the house, and playful threats were often made to him by parties wishing to draw out his eccentricities, that "they would visit him in the night and storm the old oak chest." To these threats and warnings Johnny always had one reply "He had a gun, which he would make speak to any one who attempted to enter his house, and that his oak chest was too heavy for any one to carry away, and too strong and well secured to be broken open." At length, however, that which had been matter of playful threat came to be enacted in reality. A gang of desperadoes, knowing the rich booty that would attend a successful forage, formed the design and plot to rob Johnny's treasury; and accordingly, on a certain night in 18— some half-dozen men, with faces blackened and otherwise disguised, forced their way into his residence —not, however, before the gun that he so often told of had been used, but without effect. Before the old man could load again they were in upon him; and while one part of the gang assailed Johnny and his old housekeeper, and disabled them from further interference, the other part went to the old oak chest, and with sledge-hammer and crow-bar soon made entrance into it in spite of the chains and padlocks. The booty was indeed a rich one. Heaps of gold of the guinea coinage and large quantities of silver were found therein. The extent of the hoard may be judged from the fact that one of the party nearly filled his hat with gold, and in carrying it away the weight of the coin forced out the crown and let out the gold into the road. This was at some distance from Johnny's resi- dence, and being during the night, the whole could not be picked up again, and many stray pieces were found on the spot next day. It afterwards transpired that the quantity of coin taken was so great that the gang re- sorted to the expedient of measuring their respective shares out in a pint pot, the trouble of counting it being too great. The parties who had committed the robbery were not known at the time, and there was ample opportunity for their getting nut of the country. This one of them, of the name of Robert Peel, a block printer, accomplished. With his easily acquired wealth Peel discharged several debts he had contracted, and then, through the aid of a shop-keeping friend who made for him the necessary arrangements, procured for him the necessary tickets, and secreted him till the actual moment of departure. Peel took the road to Liverpool, bearing with him a good share of the heavy booty. From Liverpool he took his departure to the States, and got clear off. Another portion of the gang repaired to Hull with similar intent. They had made all arrangements for sailing, had paid their passage, got their effects on board, were starting out of dock next morning, when they must have one more carouse before they left the shores of Old England. For this purpose they repaired to a public- house. "When drink is in, wit is out." And so it proved. The conversation of the party was such as to attract the attention of the landlord, who had seen 'an account in the newspapers 'of Johnny Steele's robbery. At length one of 'the party, in the exuberance of joyous feeling, gave as a toast, "Success to the Old Oak Chest," and thus confirming the suspicions of the landlord, he very quietly, and very properly, procured a polioe-officer, who apprehended the parties, searched them and their lug- gage, fownd a considerable quantity of money, and had them transferred to Lancashire, and other arrests fol- lowed. The men were committed for 'trial, and, on the evidence of one of them, were convieted and transported for life.

Now comes the strangest part of the story. Ono of the gang was Edward Lumb, who being duly transported to one of the penal settlements, worked in the chain- gangs, and was otherwise subjected to the rigour of a penal life. From that life he escaped ten years later. The manner of Lumb's escape is in keeping with his strange and eventful history. While working as a convict, he, with 'others, formed a plan of escape, and patiently waited for months before an opportunity offered for putting it into execution. The design was to board and seize the first vessel that might visit the settlement which should, from its size, appear likely to be manned by the number who were parties to the conspiracy. At length an opportunity offered. A light vessel came to anchor fora time near the shore, and when the crew were mainly absent from the vessel, the 'conspiring convicts, to the number of seven, managed to escape from the shore, to board the vessel, to cut the cable, and sail away. Chase was made after the runaways, but the lightness of the vessel and her sailing qualities enabled them to distance their pursuers and escape. What became of 'that portion of the crew found in the vessel when boarded the narrative from which this is written does not state; but no doubt, by some means or other, they were overcome. Z After sailing for some time the vessel was overtaken in a storm, and wrecked near the shore of what at first sight appeared to them to be an uninhabited island. Three of the seven reached the shore, the others meeting a watery grave. Their position on the island seems to have been a horrible one. Without food or other re- source, they remained until one of them died of sheer starvation; and a similar fate to the others was only pre- vented by their eating the dead body-of their comrade. During the time they were thus unnaturally subsisting, they were discovered by some of the savage natives. At first only one or two were seen, when communications, by sign, and not of the most friendly character passed; and the alarm of Lumb and his comrade, at a subsequent appearance of a large party of the natives, was so great that they took to the small boat, which bad been washed ashore from the wreck, and stood out to sea. After a time they were picked up by an East 4ndiaman, when in the last stage of exhaustion from want of food and water."--In the Indiaman they were taken to Calcutta— having first given a plausible reason for being found in the plight they were. From Calcutta, Lumb 'worked as a sailor to London, on reaching which port the captain' was so pleased with his services that he gave him two pounds. With this money he made his way to Chorley, where his mother and half-brother resided, the latter keeping a public-house. The surprise of the family at the unexpected visit of one they deemed lost to them for ever may. be 'conceived. He was hurried into the upper portion of the building, to be away from ebservation ; but an -old companion, who happened to be in the house "on the spree," saw him enter, knew him, and followed upstairs, where he accosted the runaway convict. The danger of his appearance on the scene of his old haunts was pointed out to him by the family, and the necessity for his getting away to a safe distance urgently pressed. But, no; "he felt no fear; he had risked his life often enough to get home again; he was now at home; he had come to see his friends and companions, and he would see them before he went away again." At length he was induced to go to Scotland, but in a week he returned, and, entering the cottage of a neighbour, found only the wife of his friend within. As soon as he entered he desired the woman to lock the door. "Lock the door ?" replied she, "Why- should I lock the door for you ?" Looking steadfastly at her for a.;few moments, he said, "Don't you know Ned ?" She then recognised him, and did as she was requesied, and sub- sequently fetched to him some portion of his family. During his stay at Charley he was seen and met, by ap- pointment, by several of his old cronies, to whom he related, in:amplified detail, the story told above of his escape and remarkable adventures. Three weeks after- wards he set sail from Liverpool to America, his half- brother accompanying him io the point of departure.: What was the ultimate fate of this extraordinary man;is net known, but the robbery of the "Old Oak Chest," the escape of a portion of the party with a share of the heavy spoil,ethe ,transportation for -life of Lumb, and his appearance on the ground of his former exploits, within the:time named above, are: facts within the recollection of many living, and are still talked about in the locality.

LANCASHIRE IN 1792.-A VISIT TO WARRINGTON. (Br W. A. Assam, F.R.H.S.) Urban and industrial, if not rural and agricultural, Lancashire, in the latter years of the last century, pre- sented a very different scene from that which we now see in 1887. Cotton-spinning by machinery i factories was then but in the first stage of its deielopment, and calico-weaving was all done upon the hand-loom Steam (though already used for pumping 'Water out of mines) was unknown as, a motive power in manufac- tories, and water, by means of water-wheels, drove the. machines in the mills. One Mr. William Philips, who resided at Broadway, in Worcestershire, in May, 1792, made a visit to his brother near Manchester Mr. Thos. Philips; father of Sir Thomas Philips, first baronet. He, kept a Diary of each day's experiences during the Visit', which lasted about a fortnight, and it contains some curious entries. Extracts from the Diary were contri- buted to The Antiquary, not long ago. Some of these . we copy below. Mr. Wm. Philips travelled on horse- back from Worcestershire toLancashire,and the journey occupied about three days. He arrived at his brother's residence, Shepley Hall, near Ashton, seven miles from 'Manchester, on the 15th of May, 1792. The next day he records:— "Wednesday. Went round the 'fields. and 'villages .about Shepley; saw several Coal Pitts, and a Steam Engine that Pumps the Water out of some,of the Pitts. Strange and amazing inventionl think this is!" Two days after, Mr. Philips went to the town of. Ashton-under-Lyne, in, order to go through a cotton spinning mill and other works established there. He describes them as follows:—. "It is very curious and surprising to see the Spinning Mules and Jennys, as they call them spin 144 threads at once, and will Spin one Pound of them, to so fine a thread that it will reach, according to calculation, 168,000 yards, or 95 miles and a half. Then it is weaved into aprons, handkerchiefs, &c. Likewise saw the Iron Works where they cast iron Rolls and Cylinders, and bore through an Iron Pipe the same as boring through a wood Pump. It goes by Water, and the Wheels as large as any Mill Wheels, all cast Iron except the Water Wheel; they also turn large Iron Work in a Lathe, the same as our Carpenters turn a pieCC of Wood, Very wet this after- -120611." In the town of Manchester, which Was 'traversed he next day by the visitor, conducted by his brother, Mr. Thomas Philips, the hustling appearance of. the place en MarketeDay.(Saturday) was witnessed. The party, went through a Pin Manufactory, and then inspected the old Collegiate Church. Then Chetham's Library and College were seen : • Went and saw a large Old ',School or College given and supported by one Chetham. Upstairs we saw many /tooms full of Books,' piled up like Mows to the Ceiling; and many [stuffed] Serpents, Lizards, Monkeys, &c., with many stones and balls of hair that had been taken out of Cattle when killed; with Skeletons of several sizes, and many,onriosities of different sorts; we then went down in'the Cellar and tasted the Beer [home's-brewed] that the Boys drink, which Was very good. Saw some remarkable large Loaves of Bread, and a large knife that's fixed to a Bench, to cut the Bread for Milk Snd Broth, which they have in wooden Piggins." At the quay, on the Bridgewater Canal, Mr. Philips "Saw the vessels sail into the Warehouses to load and unload; very large Warehouses, and a great quantity of Corn in them, of all sorts, Tradesmen's Goods, &c." Then he "went to the Sugar House, where they make Sugar, but they are leaving off business; had not made any for three weeks. We saw about twenty or thirty sugar- loaves, and the pots they made them in. This is a very dirty place, eight storeys high." The party next pro- ceeded to the Fustian Works, a branch of the local, tex- tile manufacture once extensive and profitable, but did not see the process, it being the dinner-hour. ' Thence the visitor was taken to look at the newly-erected county prison, the "New Bailey." He remarks on it : " This is a new-built Place, and very grand it is, too good for some that are brought there; it's more like a Nobleman's House and Gardens (walled round the out- side), to appearance, than a prison. There are several Cells with Looms in for those that are Fustian Weavers to work in, and some for Fustian Cutters; there is a hundred and twenty-four separate Cells, and kept very clean and neat. The Baths and Infirmary of Manchester were in- spected :—" Here is a hot and cold Bath for the Gentle- men, with private dressing-rooms for both; kept very clean and neat. The Infirmary is a very large, hand- some Building, with pleasant gardens to walk in, and a large water, with Iron Pallisades, before the front; went and drank ie.% with Mr. Lowe, and then to Shepley to supper." Sunday was spent in tire Country at Shepley, and on Monday, Mr. Philips revisited the Bridgewater Quay in Manchester. He wrote :—" It's astonishing to a person that never saw anything of the kind to see the business that is going on here; such quantities of Slate, Timber, Stone, and Merchandise of all sorts; the Ware- houses are very extensive, but they are well filled with one thing or other—there's not less than thirty or forty Thousand Bushels of Corn in them at one time, and large quantities of Flour, &c." Tuesday was spent in a pleasant ride in the Cheshire country, where the stranger thought the sheep singular, being small and horned. On Wednesday he made a jour- ney to Liverpool, to see the chief Lanca- shire port. He had to ride on horseback from Shepley to Manchester. There were two modes of conveyance between Manchester and Liverpool in those days—the Coach and the Packet for passengers on the Bridgewater Canal, drawn by several horses at what was deemed the fair speed of under five miles an hour. Mr. Philip went part of the way by Packet, and the rest by Coach. He quitted the boat at "London-bridge," which is where the Bridgewater Canal is crossed by the London Road, about 14 miles south of Warrington, on the Cheshire side of the Mersey. He writes "We got in the boat about eight o'clock (a.m.), and when we had gone four or five miles breakfasted in the Boat: a very fine Morning and pleasant riding. Between Manchester and London Bridge, the place where we got out, is twenty-one miles, and we went under twenty- three bridges and over nine or ten. The River Mersey runs under it. There was a gentleman went under it in a phseton and pair, just at the time we were going over him in the boat. Horsemen, Waggons, and Carts we see in other places go under. This was a very great under- taking of the Duke, and must cost an amazing sum of 'money. Got to London Bridge about one o'clock; there are four Coaches stand ready every day to take the passengers on to Liverpool and other places." The passengers dined at Warrington, and did, the remaining dozen miles by coach, arriving in Liverpool at six o'clock. The return journey was accomplished in the same manner, excepting that the coaches starting from Liverpool were all full, and Mr. Philips and his friends had to be driven to Warrington in a chaise, to meet the boat there. He found the Packet much more comfortable than the jolting coach or chaise on rough, stony roads. In the boat was a passenger who enter- tained the company with music, playing on the French- horn and violin at the same time; this was thought a very extraordinary performance, as, indeed, it was. About the packet, Mr. Philips remarks in his Diary : " This Boat has seldom less than 30 or 40, sometimes 60, 80, 100, 120, and the Captain told us he once took 129 at one time. A gentleman that was in the Boat said that these Boats, being three or four of them every day, bring the Duke in £1,500 a year, and the whole tradeing on the Canal £BO,OOO a year; this was conlirmed by the Captain and others." Respecting Liverpool, the visitor writes in terms of surprise and admiration:—" We stopt none at the Inn, but went directly to see the Shipping, which is a very fine sight indeed, and what is very extraordinary [is] to see them sail along the Streets, which they do for a great way, and in several places, which I could not have believed if I had not seen it." He noted the pulling down of the old buildings in some main streets, and the erection of grand new houses just alike. Fionting the docks some of the biggest buildings were seen :—" There's some of the highest buildings lever saw down at the Docks, where the Ships load and un- load. There's Warehouses eight, nine, ten, and eleven storeys high. I saw a sack of Corn drawn up to the top of it, and in at a door in the upper storey; there's door-places to every storey to draw the goods in at. There was at the time upwards of a thousand ships, some very large and some small, that trade to different Nations." The population ot Liverpool in 1792, when these notes were made by Mr. Philips, was between 60,000 and 70,000, a little more than a tenth of what it is now. Mr. Philips slept one night in Liverpool, at the "Golden Lion," which Was pronounced an excellent inn. The next day he went to see the fort where the soldiers garrisoning Liverpoel were exercising, and saw cannon- balls built up like the roof of a house. In the outskirts of Liverpool he saw a large number of Windmills. In the evening he went to the Theatre. The Town Hall was then a-building, of which he says :—" There's a very grand House a-being built for the Mayor to live in join- ing the Exchange, Which is a very grand building of Stone. The town in general is Brick, with stone cornice and window-frames." Two engraved views of Liver- pool as it appeared at the time of this gentleman's visit are inserted in Diliiiiken's "Description of the Country Forty Miles round Manchester," published in 1793-4. In the inland view, half-a-dozen windmills are shown, exemplifying the stranger's remark on the number of such mills at Liverpool. The number of ships belonging to Liverpool in 1793 was 606, with a total tonnage of 96,694.

CALcurrs., Tl7ESDAY.—General Roberts returns to India from Burnish on February 6, when he will proceed on a tour in the Pisheen Valley. General Arbuthnot will assume the command after General Roberts's departure. MANDALAY, WEDNESDAY,—Sir Charles Bernard returns from Rangoon on the 14th inst. General Sir Frederick 1 Roberts has postponed his visit to the ruby mines owing to the difficulty of navigating the river at the present season.

nd passed would be a source of encouragement to the ge -e oh patriot hero of Hawarden—(applause)--who, at a life and after labours which had earned rest, was still Lent on doing what he conceived to be good for his count") and his kind. He had, late in life, when nature Armee called for repose, embarked upon an undertaking, perhaps the most difficult, as it was certainly the most perilous, in his whole career—an undertaking which he must have known to be surrounded by enormous difficulties, arising Irons prejudice in part, or from ignorance, and which be must also have known would lead to the sacrifice, on hie part, of close and even tender ties of political and social re- lationship. But, undismayed by considerations such as this, and having no reward to look forward to, except a sease of duty and a belief that his countrymen would re- cognise that he was prompted by that, and that only—how- ever for a time prejudice might obscure the eyes of some— he devoted the remaining years of his life to this great en- terprise. So far as the resolution related to himself he begged respectfully to thank the meeting, and assure them that he would have nothing prouder in his career to look back to than the fact that he was thought fit to be associated with that great man in his great undertaking—an under- taking in which he (the speaker) felt an interest, because he was an Irishman, and, beyond that, because he felt that it was a policy which, if pursued to completion, was fraught with good, but not merely to the country of his birth but to the country of his adoption. (Loud applause.) They had recently been witnessing what was called a Governmental crisis. The crisis was hardly yet passed. Onevery dietinguished member of the Conservative Government had departed from its midst. It was not too much to say that the man who had left the Conservative Government was the leader of the Conservative party. (Hear, hear.) He was a very active and powerful member of the Conservative party, and Suc- ceeded in elevating into gilded obscurity men, some of whom might have been his grandfather in point of age, and be might have been engaged in what was known on academy days as " skying the old masters." (Laughter.) He (Sir Charles) would simply warn the Conservative party to take care that in ceasing to lead, Lord R. Churchill did not henceforward drive them. But the party had got fresh recruits. In the House of Commons they were not in a majority, and they were relying upon what, without offence, he might term the Unionist crutch. (Laugh- ter.) The great acquisition to the Conservative party was Mr. Goschen. There were some of these dissentient Liberals whom he would call Unionists, though he did not admit, but, on the contrary, totally denied, the right to that title. He wanted to ask these gentlemen to consider what was the probable future of that group which still claimed a separate existence for itself. He wanted to ask them whether they saw any other fate except speedy effacement by the gradual process of absorption. Thev must, Recording to their own political consciences and minds, eventually become Tories or Liberals. Which were they to be? (" Tories " and " Liberal ? "I He quite agreed with both of those gentlemen. Some would be Tories and some Liberals, and he thought that Mr. Goa- chime had set the example to that section to which he naturally belonged. (Loud cheers.) It was quite true that when the Irish policy of Mr. Gladstone was proclaimed to the world it startled some, and it took others by surprise. But, looking at the signs of political progress, they could see that it had been gaining volume and strength and solidity among the public. (Cheers.) He wanted to remind them that this Irish question stopped the way to all useful legis- lation. He wanted that brought home to the minds of the stolid Liberals of Lancashire, who thought that there was, under existing cireumstances, no pos- sibility of obtaining drastic reform in the land laws, and the amendment of the law of registration which was highly defective. He wanted to see the law sim- plified, and he wanted to see a law which would give one vote te every man, but one vote only. (Cheers) There were many other questions which came home to him, such as the amendment and extension of the Employers' Lia- bility Act,with a view to making it a permanent measure,and impossible that men should contract themselves out of it. (Cheers.) There were many other questions which came borne to him as being those in which they were all inter- ested, but Ireland stopped the way; and, therefore, it was that he wished to bring it to them that this Web question was not merely a question of doing political justice, but of removing an obstacle in the way of legislatien which would be good for those of the present and of future generations. (Cheers) Right from the day of Ireland's union with Eng- land the onion had been marked by constant and increasing protest against a measure, the carrying of which and the means employed no man could defend—the Act of Union carried by fraud and bribery of the grossest kind—(shame; —never condoned by the nation, resulting in a measure never accepted by the nation, but met by protest year after year, generation after generation, which was ever increasing in volume. (Cheers.) And the measure so carried had failed in the principle for which it was intended. The day would come when he would be looking lack upon the time in which we lived, and feel astonished that this • question should have excited the passion and prejudice to which it had given rise. What was the demand That Irishmen on Irish soil should, by a legislative body to whom powers should be devolved from the Imperial Parliament, have the right to deal with Irish questions. (Applause.) Not the creation of a co-ordinate legislative isody, or one which touched the supremacy of the Crown or Parliament. It was not a measure which sought to separate Ireland from England, but simply one giving Irishmen the power, in a subordinate assembly on their own soil, of dealing with Irish questions, which they understood better than the English House of Commons—(applause)—and which they would have time to attend to, but which the house sitting at Westminster had not. He proceeded to refer to some of the I objections put forward by the Unionists, and said one cry of ' the so-called Unionists was that if Horne Rule were granted it would commence the declene of England's greateees. He knew no object which tended to boaden the liberties of the people, which had for its object the widening of the basis on which the great institutions of the country rested, or which went to break down class privileges, of which the same thing was not slid by Conservative orators. The earns was said of Catholic Emancipation, of the Reform Act, and of the disestablishment of the Irish Church. He laughed to scorn this claim of the Conservatives or Unionists to being the special preservers of the integrity of the Empire. He asked which party in the State had done most to build up the greatness of the Empire. He wanted to know who had done most te render the blessings of living in and being subject to that Empire More widely diffused and less a matter of privilege, if it be not the Liberal party—aye, and who among them was equal to the man who now led the Liberal party? What was meant by the integrity of the Empire? He did not thine many knew at all, and others did not trouble about it. But what did it really mean? It meant, he believed; the willing assent of the subject to the Soveteign's power, or upon the power of the authority to compel obedience to its authority. (Loud cheers.) Some orators seemed to forget wbat it really meant, and that the integrity of the Empire had survived broken independen- dent Parliaments in Canada and Australia among the colonists. But they said, "We want to leave the sovereignty of the Imperial Parliament unbroken." They replied, "So do we. Wet ward giategrity as slimed a thing as you dd. We regard Awe sovereignty Of Parliament as sacred a thine as you. as,. 3 and we say out scheme will strengthen it." (Cheere.). As to its being a step' towards separation, he Bald that the Irish people bad no such an idea in their minds, and if they were insane enough to bays such an idea he wanted to ask if the position of England, of Scotlattd;Or Of Ireland would be weakened if the Home Rule Bill were passed to-morrow? In every way they would be Ctrengthened. It was not suggested that either the army or the navy should be in the Power of the Irish Government. And was it not apparent that the Irish people were not so blind as to think of such a thing. He asked them to believe that the Irish nation was not a nation of fools. (Loud cheers.) He declined to argue the question, as if they were given their natural scope of aspirations, which were creditable in themselves, namely—the right to have a potential voice in the government of their own country, and they were much too cute not to see the advantages, commercial and otherwise, of maintaining a connection with a powerful and a wealthy country such as England. (Loud cheers). He did not doubt that the Irish would be led to take a pride and an interest in the Empire, because he claimed that they bad done a very great deal in building it up. (Cheers.) It was said that to grant Home Rule would bee to constitute Rome Rule in Ireland. (Laughter.) Of all the ridiculous objections raised against the question, he believed this was the most. From what part of Ireland did this cry proceed? It proceeded from the quarter where the Protestant popula- tion was so great that if there were an attempt at persecu- tion of any kind that was the place in which they would be in the ascendancy. Whatever faults the Irish possessed in recent times, and whatoree action could be blamed, it was essentially and literally true that ,the Irish agitation had been in no sense sectarian, but' in every sense national. (Loud cheers.) Having referred to the Plan of Campaign, upon which he would not say a word in defence or other- wise, but asked them to suspend their judgment on it, the speaker described the condition of the Irish tenants, and compared their position with that of English tenants. In conclusion, he said the difficulty of the crisis was this—the Government of Mr. Gladstone had propounded their plan, and it had not in the &at instance met with the general ac- ceptance of the country. But so far from regarding that failure of general acceptance as a cause for discouragement,he thought that, looking at all the circumstances, one was en- titled to be hopeful as to the ultimate issue. Ignorance and prejudice were the great obstacles in their path, and that meeting that evening would do something to remove some of it. Their business was to keep their lamps trimmed and their swords sharpened and ready when the time came—to stand by their old principles, by their old party, and led by their Old leader. (Lend cheers.) Counciller J. FORSTER then proposed a vote:of thanks to Sir Charles Russell for his attendance and address that evening. He said he fully believed that the objects of that meeting would be attained in a very short time—that the constituency would be so educated in the subjects of Home Rule that they would work shoulder to shoulder with the one common object of returning a Liberal member of St. Helens. (Applause.) When that time came they would be fully determined on the strength of what they had heard that night and what he trusted they would hear in the future, to return without any doubt one of their own towns- I men to represent them in Parliament. (Cheers.) Mr. C. M. PERCY, seconded the motion in a strong speech, during the course of which he said he hoped that before long the chairman would be a member of Parliament— (cheers)—that Sir Charles Russell would be member of the Government, and if he was not too presunsptieus, that he (Mr. Percy) would himself be in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) He said he would rather be in a minority all his life than become disloyal and desert their grand old
leader, who still towered head and shoulders above all others. (Cheers.) :ihe_resolution was carried with great enthusiasm.

ISir CHARLES BussELL, in response, said he waa deeply grateful, and expressed the pleasure it gave him to meet 16,'Iose of his countrymen who took an interest in the stirring +tions of the day. lie only claimed one merit, and that 4wng'sit. at he lead gone where he had been asked to go—not sparing imself any trouble or exertion, and he might say that as as he was able he would continue to do so. Ions" (Cheers ) " • Charles then moved a vote of thanks•to the chairman, and it._ 'id he hoped that when they next met in such a place tbev would be able to have Mr. Sinclair in a more honourable arm more representative position than he held that night. (Ches.'s.) Mr. B. A. DRONGOOLE seconded, and suggested that a that night should be sent to copy of the resolution passer: Mr. Gladstone at Hawarden. (Cheers.) The Cmunsuar acknowledged the vote of thanks, and remarked that it was rather soon f oertaider who was to come forward at the next election. (A Voice: "You are the man," and cheers.) He was chosen to be their champion at the last election, and he was grateful for their recogni- tion that he did his best to secure the victory for them. (Cheers.) The proceedings then terminated.

ANN JANE AN' TH' 011RISAILIS SINGERS. [l3lt WILKINS IlicAwnEn.] It wur a cowd wintry neet, an it wanted nobbut a fortnit to Chrismus. I wur sittin' on one soide o' th' foyre warming' mi toes an readin' th' "Examiner" whoile Ann Jane— hoo had been bakin' some mince pies—sat at th' other soide knittin' mi a pair ov stockins. We'd nowt partiklar t' talk abeaut for a wonder, so neither on us spoke a word. Well, when I'd read th' papper, I ses to Ann Jane "Hasto had onv Chrismus singers yet, owd lass?" Hoo jumped off th' chair as if hoo'd been shot, and said "Nawe, an I dunna want ony ; quoite enoo last Chrismus. I wur nearly driven crazy wi em." Well, I declare hoed no sooner sod that bur they coome a lot ov lads and lasses to th' dur an started fur t' sing "While shepherds watch their flccks by night,
All seated on the ground, The angel of the Lord came down

And" - Ann Jane war at th' dur befooar they'd toime finish th' verse, an I 'erd her say—"Sitho, if yoa dunna goo away I'll throw a bucket o water on yoa. Haew con-pa forshame t' disturb foak i' this way." I thowt boo wu.r a bit' too sharp wi em, an I towd her it wur Chrismus toime, an a customary thing fur foak to goo eawt singin. " Doesta meeon fur *l' say," hoo sed, "ut awm gooin' t' hay a lot o lunaticks yellin' an skrikin' at th' dur ev'ry hawve heawr fur a fortnit, to say _ ,h'

nowt abeaut-th' bands ut are pom-poming aw' ti neet oer ; an listen to yon dog haew its howlin', thean knows varry weel at its a sure sign ov a deeoth." "I hope it winna be as bad as theau seems t' think," I sed. "Sitho, Efrebrhum, its aw varryweel fur thee t' i talk bike that; bus theau'rt not n ev'ry neet, or theau'd soon change thi tune." "Btu I thowt theau wur fond ov a bit ov singing." Theau doesn't call that singin', doesta? " hoo answered. " Weel," I sed, "they dun ther best, an its a good owd tune." "Ay," hoo sed, "its a good tune is • Owd Win- chester,' bur if theau had t' sit an listen to it an "Duke St? an Sovrinity, " neet after neet, theau'd think theau're havm too mich ov a good thing." Just then ther wur a knock,an when hoo oppent the' dur hoo saw a poor hawve starv't felly whoa sed he'd walked fro Manchester an wur beggin a neet's lodgin. "Hay nowt fur thee," hoo said. "Missus, fur Heaven's sake gin mi a copper, or a bit o bread—awm starvin." "1 connot help thee," boo said; " ther's too mony ut coame reawnd." "God help em, Missus," he sed, "if yoa hay sarvod em th' same as yoa're sarvin' me." This war too mich fur Ann Jane; hoo could'nt stond it, so hoo gan him a penny, an hoped he'd soon see better days. We'd two moore lots o singers an a brass band at after this t' finish th' neet up wi. Befooar wi went t' bed I sed to Ann Jane, " Didta ever yer that tale abeaut owd Ike Turner. and th' trick he played upo th' Chrismus singers?" " Nawe," hoo sed, "what wur it 7" He're a bit ov a screw wur owd Ike, an ' foal sed he wur 'curry rich. "Well, theau see's he'd gone to bed an wur just in his first sleep when they wakken't him bi singin "Angels from the realms of glory." He Feet eawt ov bed in a veery crusty temper, oppent th chamber window an sed quoite pleosantle— • Haew mony is ther on yoa?" "Ten on us altogether, Mister Turner," sed th' leader. "Just wait a minit or two; , th' owd mon sed, an closed th' window. " Theere, I alias thowt he war noan so bad as foak tried to mak him eawt to be" whispered one o ' tif singers. "Ay, I dar Say he're a dacent owd chap if one ony knew tit reet road t' get abeaut him," sed another. , Whoile they war discussin th' owd mon's charac- ter, he popped his yed through th' window and throwin a jug o water on em sheawted eawt at th' top ov his voice—"Theere, yoa con tak that an' divide it amang yoa." An he did, quoite reet too," sed Ann Jane. 'An I'll do th' same if they dtmnot show a ratio moore considerashun." Well, toime sped on. It war naiw Clirismus Eve. In less than a fortnit we'd had forty-six lots of sin- gers an abeaut ten brass bands. Ann Jane had lost aw payshuns, an wur as crabby as hoo could stick. Ev'rything seeomed upsoide daewn. Th' last two. neets we'd not been able t' get ony sleep owin to th' noise an th' din at wur made. It war abeaut hawve past nine. Ann Jane had just been to th' dur t' send some oblides away at wur singin summat abeaut th' world bein varry beautiful. "1 dunnot kno wot on earth they coome here fur, at aw," hoo sad; "I've tiowt spare, an if I had I should'nt encourage er&by givin ern owt. Awm' gooin t' tak a jug of water upstairs wi me to-neet; an if they, wakken me same as they did last neet weet em tlaro." _

Wi went bed abeaut hawve past eleven, an •wur soon in th' land of dreooms. I had'ut been sleep varry long befooar I wur wakkent bi Ann Jane diggm me• in th' ribs an sheawtin eawt, " Efray- hum ! Efrayhum ! ! doesta • yer that knoekin at th' dur ?" _

. " -Ay," I said," I yer it, but tak no notice on em, lass, they'll soon goo away." " Nawe, nawe," hoo sed, "I've not biowt a jug of water up fur newt; they'n hay t' hay it." Who crept eawt o' bed, oppent th' window, an dashed th' water on th' poor singers hoe thowt), but wur finely deceoived bi a vpice smgin eawt, "If that's th' way theau'lt gooin serve mit whentv-ver I bring a letter, yoall hay t' fotch t'next one yorsen." "Eh ! Tummas, is that thee ?" hoo sed. " Awm varg sorry, bur I thowt it wur som o thoose plaguy Chrismus singers." We'd oer slept cawrsels, an been waliken't up bi th' postman.

AWFUL DILATE AT SUTTON.—JaMes Lucas, aged thirty- seven, of Boundary-road, St. Helens, was killed at the Lon- don and Manchester Plate-glass Works at Itayenhead, under shocking circumstances, on Wednesday. Deceased started a machine called "the dix," shortly after which he was by some means drawn into the machinery and killed instantly. The body when got out presented a shocking mutilated ap- pearance. ACCIDENT AT BOLD COLLIERY: Ts EDIPLOYERS' LIA- BILITY ACT.—On Wednesday afternoon, his Honour Judge Thompson, sitting at the St. Helens County Court, heard a case in which Thomas Cain, miner, of Fleet-lane, Parr, I sought to recover £3O from Mr. Isaiah Pigott, contractor for 1 sinking pit shafts, of Carlton Villa, Lathom,.near Ormskirk, on account of personal injuries received by him at the sink- ing of a shaft at Bold Colliery, on the 24th July, 1886. Mr. IL L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. Swift, Liverpool (instructed by Messrs Brighouse, Brighouse, and Jones, Ormsktrk), defended.—Piaintiff stated that ha was engaged in the sinking of the shaft. They were at a depth of about 600 yards, when a fall of earth and stone oc- curred from the side of the shaft, which was unbricked, and about four yards above him. He was struck on the leg with a large stone, and a punctured wound inflicted, the con- sequence being that he became an inmate in the Cottage Hospital, and was not able to work for eleven or twelve weeks. Plaintiff contended tlaatAhe accident occurred through the negligence of the defendant's foremen in not seeing that the sides were made secure.—Mr. Swift urged that the foremen had done their duty, and that plaintiff ought to have removed anything he saw dangerous in the sides. It was quite as much his duty to do so as the foremen's.—After several witnesses had been heard the court adjourned. The best Temperance Drink is Rompo, a pure and healthy stimulant. HORRIBLE MURDER OF A PARAMOUR AT PENDLETON.— A horrible murder was committed on Saturday at noon in Pendleton. For about nine months a dyer named Thomas Leatherbarrow, 47 years of age, had been cohabiting with Kate Quinn, a factory operative, and after repeated quarrels he, it is alleged, killed her by striking her on the head with I a hammer. The woman was frightfully mutilated, and she had been dead some time before she was discovered. Leatherbarrow got away, but he was apprehended at the I Crescent, Salford, about four o'clock. He was in a very in- toxicated condition, and the superintendent of police re- fused to have him charged with the crime until Sunday. He wished Englishmen to dis- abuse their minds of the idea that the agita- tion in Ireland was the outcome of sAttarian feeling. It was nothing of the kind; it was in every sense national. There are some Protestants certainly who seem to think that if Ireland were granted a Parliament of her ?I'm, the first use she would make of it would 1,!,e to persecute those who are not of the Roman Catholic faith. But it seems to us that these fears are groundless. It is true that there is a great deal of hot blood in Ul- ster which is often at boiling point; but it is 'Worth considering whether this lamentable state of things does not arise rather from the aggressive action of Orangemen rather than of Catholics. It should not be forgotten that. nxcept in the province of Ulster, the Catho- lics are everywhere in Ireland in a large ma- jority, and yet it is in Ulster alone that we n.ave these furious faction fights. CYRES, in fathp.,lng the rumour as to the cause of s retire•nent from the Government,

said he was "actually better and stronger at the present time than he had been since he left the House of Commons." There is no doubt that, sensitive and high-minded as he was, he felt keenly the sacrifice that he was being called upon to make in leaving the Foreign Office; and it is not unreasonable to infer that the excitement of the past fortnight has hastened the end. While he would not be a party to a false statement being put forth as to his reason for leaving the Govern- ment, it was characteristic of him that he had not one word of reproach to utter; for no later than the, day before his death, in acknowledging a sympathetic resolu- tion passed by the Exeter Conservative Working-men's Union, he said that, while re- gretting the circumstances which rendered his retirement from the Foreign Office neces- sary, he held "as heartily as ever to the great Conservative cause." The fact that the Con- servatives were losing the services of Lord IDDESLEIGH as a Cabinet Minister was warmly discussed, and strongly condemned, alike by Conservatives and Liberals. It was looked upon as the last great mistake which Lord SALISBURY had made in his management of affairs as Prime Minister ; and every effort was made to repair the wrong, short of asking Lord IDDESLEIGH to retain the portfolio of Secretary for Foreign affairs. But "the gentle Sir STAFFORD," as it was customary to speak of him when leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons, could be firm when the question involved was one ot self-respect; and he consulted his dignity and manhood by declining to be made the football of party circumstance. He has passed, alas, Suddenly from the scene, and his removal iS felt as a personal loss by every Englishman, irrespective of party. Great, as were his talents and it should g re ate r be remembered that he wag the financial genius of his party—his character wa.g still, for of him it may be said, with a literal truthfuluess which shames flattery, that "he wore the white flower of a blameless life," and "bore without abuse the grand old name of gentleman."

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The following epigram from this week's " Punch " may be taken as a neat rap at Lord Randolph Churchill : What, out of place? Well, man, take heart of
grace, Be this your comfort till once more you win it, A man like you is never out of place—save when he's in it.

It is shocking to think that the poor woman who died at Newton Bridge Station on Thursday week, was regarded as drunk by the railway officials, who accordingly left her in the waiting room, unattended, for nearly half an hour. Men cannot in such cases do more than exercise their best judgment; but when the conclusion come to proves utterly wrong, it is none the less deplorable.

Mr. J. C. Dibb, official receiver in bank- ruptcy for the Manchester, Salford, and War- rington districts, has just been appointed official receiver for the county court district of Ashton-under-Lyne. The fact that one receiver is sufficient for such a large area suggests that there is little to receive. Thanks to Mr. Chamberlain's Bankruptcy Act, bankrupts are not, as they used to be, as plentiful as blackberries.

Our neutral contemporary, under the head- ing of "Statues of Local Gentlemen," states that Mr. Bruce Joy has "received a commis- sion to execute the statue for Bradford of Sir Matthew Wilson," and has been "en- trusted with the execution of the Balfour memorial statue for Liverpool," Bradford' and Liverpool off-shoots of Warrington! Come, we are getting on, and may hope to have a Free Library by and by. The Committee of the Earlestown Viaduct Institute have every reason to feel proud of the success which has attended their labours. On Tuesday evening the prizes were dis- tributed to the science and art students. It was stated that 85 had sat, 56 had passed, and that three Queen's prizes had been obtained. In addition to the Government certificates and awards, there is a goodly number of local prizes, so that, all round, it may be said that the right thing is being done.

Eviction is not confined to Ireland. The Corporation of St. Helens have a tenant named Edward Bonny who has taken no heed of a notice to quit. The officials have had a bonny time of it, for he has put them to the trouble of going before the magistrates to get an order to evict. Edward is averse to severing connection ; he knows when he has got a good landlord, if the Cor- poration do not know when they have a good tenant.

There are people who think they are ill used if they are compelled to pay rent. There is a woman living in Chorley who a few years ago occupied a dilapidated dwelling, and was hopelessly in arrears as to rent. The pro- perty changed hands, and the new landlord said she must either go or pay rent. " Guoa —ay, aw'll gooa," said Betty, "aw'm nod gooin to pay rent for a heawse like this." And so landlord and tenant parted to their mutual satisfaction.

Mr. John White, speaking at Latchford, on Monday evening, referred to the fact that " the offertory the other morning in a certain church when a peer of the realm, two squires of the neighbourhood with their families and households, and numerous well-to-do farmers, and others were present, only amounted to 8s 61d.". It is a pity he Aid not say some- thing more certain about that "certain church." It ought, along with the peer, to be immottalised.'

A butcher named Bradden, hailing from Liverpool, has been fined 4.0 s and costs for selling diseased meat at St. Helens. The case was a very bad one; it was given in evi- dence that the animal had died of consump- tion of the lungs, and that the meat was utterly unfit for food. The fine was a heavy penalty, but a month in gaol would have been heavier, and would have had a wholesome effect. It would have struck terror into the hearts of other bad-meat butchers.

A boy named Abrams, at Widnes, has lost his life through, becoming overpowered and poisoned by noxious . gas proceeding from a spout by the river side. This drain has been a make-shift, consequent upon ob- jection being taken to acid from certain works being turned into the town sewer. The jury condemned this improvised sewer as " a dangerous nuisance," and well they might. It is a death trap which has brought descredit upon the town, and ought instantfy to be removed.

div.p: qq,r I THE EXAMINIifi, SATURDAY, JANUARY 15. 1887..

years, and Count Von Moltke says there will be war if the military authorities cannot have their way. It is thus that "monarchs and statesmen" try to bamboozle the people. But the Germans are not to be walked over in this way. They decline to pass the Army Bill in this objectionable form.

If the people would only take military matters more into their own hands they would soon see the folly of burdening themselves with big standing armies. This is a point which Mr. John Crosfield has made up his mind to drive home. He was hammering at it on Tuesday night at the annual conference ot the Financial Reform Association ; and he hit the nail on the head when he said—"lt was perfect nonsense to talk of any other people comi:ig over to take England."

How is it that the clergy leave it so much to laymen to preach peace on earth and goo I will to men ? Dissenting Ministers do some- times improve the occasion when we are in the hurly-burly of a wicked war—such for in- stance as that with Afghanistan—but State preachers are for the most part silent. Is it because they are State preachers—because they are conscious of their servitude as ser- vants of the State? Disestablishment would make them free men in this respect. How long will they cling as they do to a State Church, "chains, and slavery."

"Now surely at last it will be generally re- cognised how utterly unsuitable a place is the House of Commons for the discussion of sub- jects relating to the spiritual domain of the Church. What the Church assuredly requires for her well-being and due development is the powcr of regulating ber own spiritual affairs." This is what the Rev. J. Sheepshanks said, in his annual sermon on Sunday last, at St. Margaret's, Anfield, and we say " Amen to that."

INDUCTION OF THE ARCHDEACONS OF LIVERPOOL AND WARRINGTON.-At the Liverpool pro-Cathedral on Tuesday evening special service Was held for the formalinduction to the archdeaconry of Liverpool of the Venerable John Waring Bardsley, late Arch- deacon of Warrington and vicar of St. Saviour's, Falkner-square, and of the Rev. Canon W. Lefroy, vicar of St. Andrew's, Renshaw-street, to the arch- deaconry of Warrington, viee Ardhdeacon Bardsley. The new Archdeacon of Liverpool succeeds the Ven- erable Archdeacon Jones, who has resigned owing to old age, being nowin his 96th year, and who, it may be mentioned, is the oldest clergyman in the diocese, his ministrations in Liverpool dating from the time of the battle of Waterloo. The clergy Who took part in the induction service were conducted to their stalls by the Rector of Liverpool (Canon A. Stewart), the head of the Chapter. The Bishop (Dr. Ryle) occupied the episcopal throne, and the stalls ' were occupied by Canons Burbridge (St. Michael's- in-the-Hamlet), H. Jones (Waterloo), Woodward (St. Silas's), Blundell (Halsall), M'Neill (St. Paul's, Prince's Park), Livingstone (Aigburth), Lester (St. Mary's, Kirkdale), Postance (Holy Trinity, Toxteth Park), Cross (Southport). and Eyre (St. Helens.) Archdeacon Bardsley, having taken his seat as Arch- deacon of Warrington, the Rector led him by the hand to the stall vacated by the late Archdeacon of Liverpool, and formally inducted him therein; and in a like manner Canon Lefroy was formally induced into the stall belOnging to the Archdeaconry of War- rington, vacated by Aychdeacon Bardsley. The ordinary evening service was celebrated. Canon Cross read the first lesson, Canon A. Stewart the second lesson, and the prayers and collects wore read by the Rev. C. M. Wardldw. The musical por- tion of the service was Stewart s, in " G," and the anthem was Mozart's "Judge me, 0 Lord." There was a large congregation, which included a number of clergymen.
