LANCASHIRE AND Yens:smuts BANK, LIMITED.— The report of the directors of this bank has just been issued. From it we gather that the directors propose a dividend of 10 per cent, clear of income tax, on the year, and to add•• 1,5,000 to the reserve fund, and also carry forward a balance of £4,028. The reserve fund will, therefore, be increased to £120,000. The retiring directors are Alderman Joseph Davies, J.P., of Warrington, and Mr. Samuel Rigby, J.P., of Chester, both of whom are proposed for re-election. IMPROVID.IRNT IN THE IRON TRADE.—The Eng- lish iron market has been more active during the' , past fortnight than is usual at this time of yeas,. The improvement has been most marked in pig- iron, and prices of crude iron have been substan- tially advanced. It is open to question, however, whether the full rates now paid will be maintained, as much speculative buying is going on. The 1 lasgow warrant market has bees very excited since the year came in, a large business has been doing, and the price has risen 3s per ton. So far the Scotch pig-iron trade has not responded, but, in sympathy with warrants, maker's iron is very strong. Closing buyers of warrants were on Wed- nesday 47s 4d cash and 47s 'rid a month, sellers wanting one halfpenny per ton more. The northern pig-iron trade has also been very much firmer since the year commenced, and prices have advanced 3s to 3s M per ton.---/roe. Title PROPOSED Cauricu Hoqa.E.-- The "Libera- tor," referring to the opposition of the Bishop of Worcester and others to the building of the pro- posed Church House, on-the ground that the money to be Spent upon it would be better employed in improving the incomes of the poorer clergy, says: —"lt is very obvious from criticisms such as these that the Church House will not be built without giving rise to feelings amongst a large number of the clergy which will do anything but strengtheni the existing system." And it adds, with reference to the Archbishop of Canterbury's championship of the scheme :-." We venture to suggest that the Archbishop is probably taking time by the forelock in view of coming eventualities in the direction of disestablishment. 'He cannot but know how the tide of 'public opinion is running; and he no doubt believes that more compactly organised than it is at present, and no longer 'homeless,' the Church, would be far better prepared than it is now for the shock of disestablishment when it comes." i

UNKNOWN AND UNCARED FOR AT RUNCORN. I Mr. J. B. Worsley, the deputy coroner. on Saturday morn- I Inv, held an inquest at the office of the Burial Board on the body of a man unknown, who died on Friday morning at a common lodging-house In Fryer-street, kept by Patrick I Phillips. Mr. J. W. Lightburn was foreman of the jury. Phillips deposed that the deceased came to his house on the j let Inst. He was a man about six feet high, and appeared to be healthy and strong. He was poorly dressed. His luggage c‘neisted of a hare containing a hammer, a few chisels, and odds and ends; and he "went about mending machines." On Thursday night, about eleven o'clock, Phillips found the deceased lying on the bedroom floor, sick. He asked him what he had been doing to tusks a mess , like that: but the man returned no answer. As he was I not in a fit state to get int) bed Phillips took off his coat, clogs, and stockings, and left him lying on the floor with only his shirt and trousers for a covering. Subsequently -Phillips heard the man moaning and saying "0 ! Jesus," bet no notice was taken of him. Next morning at half- past eeven the man was lying on the floor dead. Phillips said he treated the man as though he was drunk, although he bad appeared all right on going upstairs. There was no I fire in the room.—A stone-breaker, named Henry Jones, of Liverpool, who bad lodged at Phillip's house since Monday, deposed that on Thursday night the deceased came to bed ' about half-past nine. When he entered the room he stag- gered against witness's bed, and then fell upon the floor, witness, although rather deaf, hearing him snore heavily. J The deceased showed all the appearances of drunkenness.— Dr. McDougall said he had made a post morteni examination of the body that morning. The stomach, live., and kidneys were very much diseased, and the lungs were highly conges- ted. In his opinion the condition of the lungs were the cause of death. The organs of the body appeared to be those of a heavy drinker. The exposed condition in which the deceased was left in the room on a cold, frosty night would conduce too-x.l)ld conjestion of the lungs. An expo- sure of that kidd would have been a serious risk to a thoroughly healthy person.—P.C. Povey deecrihed the clothing of the deceased, and said he found a purse contain- ing is 3d in his pocket. There was nothiog whatever to Identify him.—The jury returned a verdict that death was the result of natural causes.

TREAT TO AGED PERSONS AT RUNCORN. The annual treat to the aged poor persons of Runcorn was given on Tuesday evening in Runcorn Public Hall. "I his is the fifth year the Young Men's Christian Association has entertained the old folks to a repast abundant and whole• some, and the success of the venture in the pleasure afforded to the numerous guests has each year amply re- paid the young men for the trouble involved. It is to be regretted that as far as finances go theassociation is not in a very flourishing condition, and had the welcome hospitality depended upon their funds it could not have been dispensed. The tradespeople and gentlemen interested in the town have, however, freely given of their substance to the worthy object, and on the present occasion the generosity has been more pronounced than ever. The sum of £32 was collected by a committee appointed for the purpose, consisting of Messrs S Coventry, J A Smith, FJ Norman, C N.c,s .n, J E Meredith. and Mr W Pownall. Jun.. secretary ; and t hrough the solicitations of Messrs Coventry, Smith, and Woodl pad provisions and fruit to the value of £2O were also contribu- ted. Having the wherewithal, tbe organisation of the treat remained with the Young Men's Christian Asooci,tioe. and with the aid of numereus voluntary workers it we carried out to a successful issue. Ace was the only passport needed to admit a person to the capital tea pro: ided, in which beef and ham, with bread and butter, were the principal with a finish of sweet breads of various desc;ipti .us. Sixty, years was the lowest limit fixed, but many below that age were doubtless admitted, and the total number of persons present when the repast commenced was about 700. Many Were too infirm with age, or through some accident of life, to walk to the hall, and these were conveyed in cabs acting under the directions of Messrs Cooke, Isgltielal, and Greaves. The oldest person present WAS a woman, whose hair had beon whitened with the frost of .•.13 winter., and there were not a few who had overstepped the allotted span ' of man upon the earth. As usual, Mr John Simpson took a lively interest in the proceedings, and was dbcovered hav- ing a chat with more than one 'old crony ;" while the presi- dent, Mr F A Lake, the vicar, the Rev A Maitland Wood, curpo da and derwe waiters, whilst btyheq the curate, the Rev W W K Ormsby, the Rev George Ward, and others freely mixed with those present. div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

FAILURE AT WIDNES.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, Mr. Registrar Bellringer granted a re- ceiving order on the petition of John Merrick, milliner, draper, furniture dealer, and journeyman, of 42 and 62, Wid- nes-road, Widnes. WIDNES TONTINE SOCIETY.—The members of the Mersey Mutual Society have each received 20s 4d after the various sick and burial claims have been satisfied. The Mersey Hotel Tontine has had an income of £lB6 17s, and an ex- penditure of £l2 2a 4d. The division of the money yields las 3d to each full member. SUDDEN DEATH AT HALEBANK.—Mrs. Mercer, wife of Mr James Mercer, Lenor Farm, Halebank, died suddenly on Tuesday night. A fortnight ago she was confined, but under the care of a pretessional she was progressing very favour- ably until Tuesday night,whea she complained that she was choking, and in ten minutes death ensued, DENSt FOG AT WIIMES.—A dense tog hung over Widnes last evening, and traffic of all descriptions was rendered very difficult. About half-past five a boatman employed on the flat Express walked into Widnes dock, but there beira numerous persons in the vicinity, his cries quickly brought bitn aid, and be was rescued very little the worse for his dip. Ha. ALEXANDER PRESTON, 8.A., M.R.C.S., brother to the Vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, who was desperately wounded at the battle of Maiwand, during the late Afghan war, when in charge of the 6dth Regiment, has been pro- moted from the rank of surgeon major to that of brigade surgeon, Dr, Preston received the Afghan medal for gal- lantry in the field. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—Uneler the auspices of this society, Mr. H. Wade Deacon delivered an interesting lecture, en. titled" Homes without hands," in the National School, on Thursday night. There was a capital attendance, The lec- ture was descriptive of the habits of animals, birds and in- sects, and was admirably illustrated by an oxy-hydrogen limelight lantern manipulated by Mr. Driffield.

INSPECTION OF POLICE AT WIDNES.—OR Tuesday the Chief Constable of Lancashire (Colonel Moorsome) in- spected the police force of Widnes in the Drill Hall. There were present Inspector Wood, five sergeants (Robinson, Clarkson, Strickland, McGregor, and Brydges), and 31 constables. Three constables were on duty. Toe in- specting officer expressed himself highly satisfied with all he saw. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—A labourer, named Jonathan Hughes, was severely scalded on Wednesday, at the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Hughes was employed at the new works, and while following hie work he was scalded upon both arms by some vitriol. In his agony the man made an attempt to jump into the canal, but was prevented by P.C. Hoyle. He was carried home on a stretcher, and is now under the care of Dr. MacDou- gall. A CHAPEL ON FIRE AT WIDNES.—About half-past five on Thursday morning the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Simm's Cross, was discovered to be on fire that part known as the boiler-house. An alrrm was raised, but the aid of the fire engine was not needed, as the flames were extin- guished by means of buckets of water. Oo the previous evening a tea party had been held in the building, and it is conjectured that some heated cinders must have fallen on the flooring and set it alight. The damage is of trifling amount. CHRIST CHURCH, WESTON POINT.—The annual congre- gational tea party was held in the schoolroom on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance. Subsequently an entertainment was held under the presidency of the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson, the incumbent, who dealt with the work of the parish during the past year. Matters had gone most satisfactorily in every respect. In the concert the, follow- ing took part :—The Chairman, Messrs. P. C. Rosenberg, R. Morris, N. Grounds, T. Grounds, W. Grounds, Miss Towns, Miss M. Clarke, Miss L.Mathers, and Miss Jones.

ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. BRTINDRIT'S WORKS, RUNCORN.—. Yesterday morning a serious accident occurred at the shipl building yard of Messrs. Brundrit and Co. A number of men were employed shifting timber by means of a travelling crane, which stands at a height of about 20 feet, when some part of the machinery gave way, and Thomas Wil- liamson, of Queen-street, was precipitated to the ground. Aeother man named Hitchmough had a narrow escape. Both Williamson's arms were fractured, his nose was broken, and other parts of his body were seriously injured. He was conveyed home on a stretcher, and a doctor was immediately called in attendance. DEATH OF AN OLD DITTON BESIDENT.-139, the demise of Mr. John Fazackley, of Bank Buildings, Hough Green, which took place last week, the village of ditton has lost another of its old inhabitants. Mr. Fazacklev, who was over SO years of age, was born in Ditton, and has during the whole of his lifetime resided in that village. He was well- known, and in his younger days was considered to be the beet runner and jumper for miles around. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon at Earnworth, the ceremony'be- ing ;performed by the Rev. James Lawton. As evidencing the longevity for which Ditton is so remarkable, we may state that the deceased's brothers, James and William, were aged 89 and 84 respectively. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. W. H. Rogerson. Present—Messrs. James Handley. J.P., H. Coleburn. G. Moss, W. Littler, W. Whittaker, E. Imison, land W. F. Salkeld (secretary.)—The Chairman reported Ithat the interments for nine months ending December 25th. were 242, a decrease of two on the corresponding period of 1885. The fees received during the same period amounted to £248 7s Bd. a decrease of 10d on the previous year.—The report of the Finance Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr. Moss, seconded by Mr. Littler, stated that the receipts for the past month amounted to £43 Os 23, of which £8 lie had been paid in wages. and the balance paid into bank. Accounts amounting to £8 2s 10d were passed for payment. There was no other business. INTERCHANGE OF PULPITS AT RUNCORN.—On Sunday night last there was a general interchange of pulpits at the Nonconformist chapels in Runcorn. The Rev E Williams (Presbyterian) preached at St Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, his own pulpit being occupied by the Rev T Lagar (Primitive Methodist.) The pulpit at the Greenway-road Primitive Methodist Chapel was occupied by the Rev A P Watson ( Wesleyan ) The Rev R F Hornabrook (Wesleyan) preached at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, while the Rev J D Thomas (Congregationalist) discoursed at the Halton-road Wesleyan Chapel. The Rev George Wood preached at the United Methodist Free Church, while the pastor, the Rev E Hall, was at the Wesleyan Chapel. On Monday night there was a united communion service in Bethesda Chapel, when addressee were delivered by the Revs G Wood and E Williams. Prayer meetings have also been held at the dif- ferent chapels. HALTON AND THE QUEEN'S JuEILEE.—A public meeting of the inhabitants of Halton, Norton, Stockham, Clifton, and Astenoor, called by circular, was held in her Majoe'y's Ancient Court Lest Room of Halton, on Wednesday even- ing, when there was a good attendance. The Vicar pre- sided. and briefly stated that they had met together to con- sider matters in relation to the Jubilee, so far as concerned their own parish. Far and wide the varieus public bodies were moving to show their loyalty and attachment to their beloved Queen on such an auspicious occasion, and Halton could not be behindhand, inasmuch 39 Queen Victoria was "Baron " of Halton, and was annually represented at the Court Lest by her High Steward, Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington; Halton Castle too, being the property of the Queen, by virtue of her office aa "Duke" of Lancaster. The Chairman then invited free and open discussion, after which it was unanimously resolved that the Jubilee should be kept in Halton in a manner befitting the "golden" occa- sion. A large committee, composed of representatives from every- part of the parish, was formed, and a secretary ap- pointed. The meeting closed by singing the National Anthem.

Mrs 6 Wood, Mrs Wood (vicarage), Mrs Whittaker, Mn Marwood, Mrs Lake, Mrs Rogerson. Mrs Hankinson, Mrs White, Miss Peacock, Miss Norman, eke., with the bon. secre- tary, Mr W Pownall, jun. The Chairman delivered a brief introductory address, in I which he gave all a hearty welcome, and said there was not a day In the year looked forward to with more pleasure by the members of the Y.M.C.A. than the one on which they could show honour to grey hairs, and do something to I lighten the hours of their older fellow-townsmen and towns- women. (Applause.) In concluding he wished those pre- sent a bright and happy new year. 'During the interval in the programme fruit was distribu- ted amongst the audience, and the Rev.4.A. Martlaod Wood made a speech. He referred to the fact that he and his curates were strengers amongst them and said the kindly welcome that had been extended to :hem had made them sure that whatever else the people of Runcorn were they were at any rate extremely warm-hearted kindly folk. (An- plans%) After being there not quite a fortnight he felt that he might call himself a proud man in being Vicar of Run- corn. (Applauee.) Be hoped they would understand that he and his colleagues had come amongst them as their servants, and that they were there for the express purpose of doing all the good they possibly could without any dis- • tinction of class or person. (Hear, bear.) They hoped to he able to do whatever they would permit them to do for their benefit, and to help them both in their concerns of this world and the world to come. (Applause.) Alluding to the treat, the vicar said this entertainment of the old • people was a most happy thing. He understood all those present had to be 60 years of age. He did not think they , were by their appearance, bat if they were, Runcorn must be one of the healthiest places on the face of the earth. (Lauehtee and applause.) He went on to point out that al- though they were old they could still do much useful work, and added that the true secret of happiness was in trying to do what was useful to other people. (Applause.) The following programme was gone through :-3ong•, "Old England is old England still," Mr. Bates; "Hen con- vention," and "Father, what have you got for no ?" Mr.P. Shaw; Lancashire recitations, Mr. Elias Davies, " Pat , Malone" and The cruise of the Calabar ;" "Carrier John," Miss Nellie Haedley ; "Mocking bird," Mr. A. Fox; I dttet, "Courtship." Miss Horton and Mr. Morris; duet. "The gipsy countess," Miss Howard and Mr. Mortis ; and concertina solo, Mr. Wilton. The 2nd C.R.V. Band played several selections, and the Parish Church Handbell Ringers gave two performances. The duties of accompanist were performed by Miss Fanny Handley, Mr G. Howard and Mr. C. Pownall. The audience frequently testified to their en- joyment and appreciation by bearty applause and recalls, the comic element meeting with most favour. The man- agement of the treat, it may be stated, was in the hands of a committee, composed of Messrs. Meredith. Norman, Shaw, and W. Pownall, jour. The proceedings concluded at half- past nine by the singing of the national anthem, accompa- nied by the band.

div.head: SUFFOCATED BY SEWER GAS AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUFFOCATED BY SEWER GAS AT WIDNES.

A sad fatality occurred at Widnes on Wednesday morn- ing, the victim being William Thomas Twiss, 14 years of age, who resided at 13, John-street. The youth got up about seven o'clock, and having started a tire in the grate, and prepared the table for breakfast, he went out without informing his mother where he was going. Three hours later his dead body was brought home on a stretcher. It seems that about nine o'clock a man named George Barkley saw a dead body lying on the shores of the Mersey on Widnes Marsh, and thinking it had been washed up by the tide, be did not make an examination, but at once went to tbe police station. Sergeant Chat kson and Constable Thomp- son immediately proceeded to the spot, and were surprised to discover that the body had not been in the water, and was quite warm, The officers adopted Dr. Sylvester's method of restoring animation to the apparently dead, but without effect, and electric shocks administered by Mr. L. Kilcross were also of no avail. Dr. Richards now came upon the scene and pronounced life extinct, probably through suffocation by sewer gas, with which the youth's lungs were tilled. When discovered the body was lying near to the outlet of a sewer which drains away the waste products of the numerous chemical works en the marsh. The identity having been established, the body was removed to John-street to await a coroner's inquiry. The inquest on the body was held at West Bank Hotel, by Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner. Mr. J. C. Routledge watched the proceedings on behalf of the trustees of the late Mr. John Hutchinson —Margaret Abrams, wife of Mr. Charles A. Abrams, clerk, of 13, John-street, deposed tl;at the deceased was her son. He had been in the habit of gathering sticks on the river side, but on this °melon she believed be went to endeavour to get a situation at the saw mills.—A boy named Herbert, who lives in White-street, stated he 8,11,7 the deceased go on the docks.—George Bartley, a Waterman, who lives in Mersey-road. stated that be found the deceased about a quarter past nine. He was lying on the high water- mark about 30 yards from the outlet of the main sewer, and about two yards from the end of a " wooden spout." As be thought the body bad been washed ashore by the tide, wit- ness did not go near it, but went to the police station. He described the efforts made by the officers to animate the boy's torm, when they found that it was warm. The gas from the "wooden spout" was very strong, and they had to remove the boy a distance before they could make any efforts to revive him.—Sergeant Clarkson having given evi- dence. Mr. Routledge aaid the " spout" was a sewer used by about five manufacturers, who turned acid into it. The I acid used to be drained into the main sewer, but the Noxious , Vapours Inspector bad said this practice was detrimental to I health, and Hutchinson's trustees then gave the manufac- I torero the privilege of making this small drain.—A juryman questioned the right of the manufacturers to pour such ob- noxious liquid into the river, but Mr. Routledge said the river at that point was considered as the sea, and they could pour anything into it —The Coroner said it was not right that the sewer should be In its present condition, be- cause it was a danger to all persons who went along the river side, and their lives might be brought to an untimely end like this poor boy's.—After some conversation, the jury returned a verdict that the bo-y was accidentally suffocated by the gas from the sewer, and added a presentment that the condition of the sewer was a dangerous nuisance.

div.head: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITrEE.
div.p: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITrEE.

A meeting of this committee was held at Alforde Chant. hers last evening. Mr H W Deacon presided, and there were present Messrs E Carey. F Heyes, B Brown, S Sadler, R Davies, R Lewis, and J T Allen (clerk to the Local Board).

div.head: TENDER.
div.p: A TENDER.
The committee appointed to consider the tender for the supplying of books worth about £3OO, recommended that the tender of Mr T Laurie. of London, be accepted.
THE RULES.-TERMS OF BORROWING.

The rules were again under consideration, and some dis- cussion ensued as to non-residents who worked in the town haying the privilege of berrowing.—The Chairman pointed out that if non-residents could not borrow, Mr. Lewis, although a member of the committee, would be unable to take advantage of the Library.— Mr. Brown did not think anybody who did not pay rates should have the privileges of the ratepayers for whose bene- fit the library was established.—Mr. Mattison said if a man outside the township invested capital in a shop, he could borrow, but a workingman whose labour was his capital if he lived over the ditch in Ditton could not borrow.—The Chairman weld ther were not following the good example set them by St. Helens. He did not think they ought to be narrow in a matter of this kind.—Mr. Carey said if thy made a rule that none but ratepayers should borrow' the rule would be evaded by persons who lived in the town borrowing for their friends outside, and the committee would only get the discredit of being narrow. I —Mr. Reyes moved that only ratepayers and residents in Widnes have the privilege of borrowing, and that non-resi- dents should pay an annual sulrcription of 10s.—Mr. Mor- rison : A shilling a year will be amplo.—Ultimately Mr. , Heyes proposed that the charge be Gcl per quarter, and then Mr. Sadler seconded his motion.—Mr. Morrison (to Mr. Lewis) : What do you think ?—Mr. Lewis : I think it is mean.—Mr. Carey: I think it would be meaner to charge more.—The Chairman pointed out that under the rule pro- Pesed by Mr. Heyea, any person wherever he lived could borrow books.—The resolution was, afterwards altered that the charge should be made to persons employed in Widnes, but living outside. books being lent out free to residents.— Mr. Carey said he should prefer that the library should be free to all persons who worked in Widnes, and he did not think the sum they should get was worth considering; and the rule would besides be evaded.—Tbe Chairman sAd Mr. Allen had pointed out to him a clause in tha Free Libraries Act which stated that the neighbouring parishes could join with the town in their library by the raterayers agreeing in public meeting to contribute towards the rate. This rather supported the contention that outsiders should pay something towards the use of the library.—Mr. Lewis : In a corporate manner.—Mr. fleyes : And as they cannot at pre- sent we propose to let them do it individually.—The motion was carried. Mr. Carey did not vote.

div.head: FELONIES AT WIDNES.
div.p: FELONIES AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. Brock and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Police Court on Monday, Richard Rawlinson. a labourer. aged 19, pleaded guilty to having, on the 18th ult., stolen a pair of boots, value 3s 3d, from the door of tha shop of Thomas Hall, boot manufacturer, Waterloo-road. A tine of • 20s, or 14 days' bard labour, was Prss- cot, a labourer, who lives at the " Model," Waterloo-road, was charged with stealing a shawl and a pair of boots, value 4s 6d, from the person of Catherine Carey, a widow, who lives in Lugsdale-ro ad. On the night of the 18th ult., as Mrs. Carey was walking along Lugsdale-road, carrying the articles mentioned, the prisoner snatched them out of her hands and ran away. The WOMAD was locked UD on some charge the same ni4ht, and could not consequently search for the thief; but on being liberated from goal she saw him. He acknowledged that be had pawned the shawl and sold the boots, and asked the woman to say nothin about the matter, and be would redeem the shawl. The pri- soner was fined 20s, or in default go to gaol for 14 days.— ' Jun., Dittos, Mr. J. W. domestic servant, 15 years of age, was charged with haviegg stolen la ld in money, and two jackets and a dress worth Id, the property of Michael Cassidy, A nne.street East. Th prisoner had been employed as a servant to Mrs. Cassidy. On Friday night, the prisoner and 1s Id from a drawer were missing, and Mrs. Cassidy went to the London and North- Western Railway station, where she found the prisoner with a ticket for Liverpool in her possession, and also the two jackets and dress, She was given into Custody. A Mrs. Humphreys deposed to having given the prisoner Is 6d with which to go to Liverpool and see her mother, and the pri- soner contended that Mrs. Cassidy had given her the cloth- ing. The magistrates considered there was a doubt in the case, and discharged the prisoner.

div.head: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.

The annual meeting of the members of this bank was held at the office iligb-ttreet, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. S. Brundrit, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were present... the Rev. W. Preston, Rev. E. Williams, Messrs. J. Simpson, J. Handley. S.F., F. A. Lake, W. H. Rogerson, J. Pritchard, W. Littler, and W. Handley (actuary.)

div.head: LATE PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE LATE PRESIDENT.

• The Rev. W. Preston proposed the following resolution "The trustees and managers of the Rnncorn Swings Rank , plane on record thrir appreciation of the services rendered' to theissith Its late lamented president the Rev. Canon"' Barmy, he having for the lengthened period of, 40 years presided almost uninterruptedly over, its annual meetings, and in every way evinced the greatest interest in its affairs." Mr. Preston remarked that he was thoroughly in sympathy with that resolution, Ind endorsed every word of it. • - _ _ _ _

The Rev. E. Williams seconded the resolution. He had he said, koewnithe late vicar for nearly 20 years, and to know him was to esteem and rozard him most highly. The resolution was carried unanimously' and it was decided to forward a copy to Mrs Barclay and family.

div.head: TRE REPORT.
div.p: TRE REPORT.

The actuary teed the following report:—" i beg respect- fully to submit the following report, being an epitome of the transactions of the bank for the year ending November 20th, 1886. Daring the year 142 new accounts were opened, 39 closed accounts were re-opened, and 85 ac- counts were closed. At the close of the year 837 accounts were open with the bank, being an increase as compared with the previous year of 93. These accounts were held as follows :—Personal depositors 765, penny banks 3, charit- ahle e,ciyties 20, friendly societies 49, total 837. There has been a marked increase during the year in the number of friendly societies accounts, the number being 49 as com- pared with 39 for the previous year. Tne total number of depes,:s was 1,771, and of withdrawals GOO, giving a total of 2,371 separate transactions, being en increase of deposits as compared with last year of 85. and a decrease of with- drawals of 42. The total amount deposited was £7,393 3s lid, and withdrawn £6,309 18a 10d. Of these amounts £2,650 16s 10d was deposited as follows :—Friendly sods- ` ties, £2,016 lOs - charitable societies, £358 7s 6d ; penny banks, £275 19s Id. The amount withdrawn by societies was £2,238 2s 7d, as follows :—Friendly societies, £1.613 Os 3d; charitable societies, £395 7s 5d ; penny banks, £229 a 14s 11d. The average deposits exCludieg societies, was t £3 13s 6.1, and withdrawn zr-rirap. The sam of 4073 17s 6d .has been added daring the year to the depositors' accounts for interest and dividends on stock. The amount held by the bank at tie close of the year on account of depositors was as follows : Personal depositors, £20,704 14s 7d; penny banks, £535 16s 6d ; charit- able societies, £269 9s lid; friendly. societies, £4,855 9s 3d; total £26,365 10a 3d. To meet this the amount held on ac- count of the bank by the National Debt Commissioners at the same time was £26,017 18s 4d, and with £385 15s 8d held by the treasurer gives a total of £26,403 14s. The position of the bank at the aim of the year was improved by an increase of £2,263 103 41 in the amount An& to de- positors, and 96 in the number of open accounts. Daring the a ear a perchase of Government stock was made by the hank for a depositor under the provisions of the Act of 1880, the price paid, including commission on purchase, be- ing £99 12s 3d for £lOO of new 3 per cents., the dividends on which are received and credited by the bank without cost to the depositor, thus securing a rate of a little over 3 per cent. on the investments. These class of invest- ments enable those who have more to deposit than £3O per year, or £l5O in the whole to in- vest through the bank £lOO in any one year or any smaller amount not less than £lO up to a total of £3OO in Government stock, the bank as shown above, receiving and crediting their accounts with the half- yearly dividend. The attention of depositors is drawn to the little known, yet important provisions of a recent Act of Parliament (The Provident Nominations and Small In- testaries Act 1883) which varies and enlarges the posses- sions hitherto vested in Trustee Savings Boas in respect to deposits of intestates. The whole of the section of the Act reads as follows: A depositor in a savings bank not being under sixteen years of age; may by writing under hit hand, delivered at or sent to the effic,e nominate any per- son not being an officer or servant of the hank (unless such officer or servant be the husband, wife, father, mother, child, grandchild, brother, sister, nephew, or niece of the nominator), to'whom any sum not exceeding £lOO, which may remain due to such depositor at his decease, may be I paid at such decease, and may from time to time I revoke or vary such nomination by writing under his hand similarly delivered or sent; and on receiving satisfactory proof of the death of a nominator, the dtrectors shall pay to the nominee the sum doe to the deceased depositor, pro- vided it does not exceed £lOO Previous to the passing of this Act no larger sum than £5O caLli be paid to the repre- sentative of a deceased depositor without the production of probate or letters of administration." Mr. W. H. Rogerson moved the adoption of the report. Dr. MacDougall seconded the motion, and remarked that it must be gratifying to all interested in an institution of that description to find that it had been so successful during the past year, when the incidance of labour had been 90 tight, and mach a large number of people, although not out of employment, had certainly lessened incomes. It showed strongly that there was a spirit of thrift in the district. He was glad to hear that the friendly societies were taking ad. vantages of the facilities offered by the bank to deposit their money, and were thus receiving considerable interest, and encouraging thrift amongst their own members and other persons. The report was adopted unanimously. Mr. James Handley proposed a vote of thanks to the trea- surer, Mr. Simpson, for his services during the past year. It was, he said, in cons,quence of the careful work of their excellent treasurer that the bank had shown such excellent results.

Mr. Lake seconded the motion, which was carried by ac• clamation, In acknowledging he vote, Mr. Simpson said he should be glad if they could find someone to take his place. He was glad the bank was going on so satisfactorily. Its con- dition spoke well for the management of the present actuary. Since the year plosed he bad invested £7OO, so that the -- business of the bank was still going in an upward direction. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pritchard proposed with much pleasure that Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., be appointed president in the room of the late Canon Barclay. This, he urged, would be a most fit- ting and appropriate appointment, and would receive the ap- proval of the whole of the depositors, and would induce confidence M the minds of the public at large. Mr. James Handley seconded the motion, and referred to Mr. Brundrit's long connection with the bank. Mr. Bran- drit had always evinced a very warm interest in the bank, and had devoted many hours of labour to its benefit. He was one of the oldest, if not the oldest, depesitors in the bank. The proposition was carried unanimously.

The Chairman expressed his warmest thanks for the hon— our they had conferred upon him. It was quite true that he - was ono of the oldest depositors. He thought the first - money placed to his account was in 1847, and it remained in the bank still, so that no one could accuse him of not be- ing lo,ral from the beginning. His best wish for the insti- tution was that it should flourish in the future as it had done in the past. Be did not sea why it should not when it had got the well merited confidence of the public. With such a staff as they had, and with their old friend, Mr. Simpson, as treasurer, and Mr. Handley as actuary, lie did not doubt its future prosperity. (Applause.) The Rev. E. Williams moved the appointment of Mr. W. F. Salk4d as vice-president. His past faithfnl connc cion 'with the bank wia an augury that this services in the fu- ture as vice-pres;dent would be of benefit. Mr. W. Littler seconded the preposition wifh great pleasure, and r.ferred in complimentary terms. The motion was carried unanimously:

... .„.. -- The auditors, Messrs. J. H. Salk4d, E. Marwcod, W. Brookes, and 'W. Williamson Isere re-appointed; and 1. vote of thanks hitvin been passed to the chairman on thA pro- position of Mr. Simpson, seconded by Dr. MacDougall, the meeting terminated.
A. collision occurred between moda trains near Re;ford on Thursday morning, one train falling over an embankment. lhe injury caused is slight.

Dr. Duggan, one of the sanitary officers of the Lorgan Union, reported to the Lurgan Guar- di ins a few days ago that he had visited the of Pat McConnell, Cloncere, County Armagh. The house, which was in a shocking state, consisted of one apartment only, but its inhabitants were 14 in num- ber—Pat, his wife, and 12 pigs. The guardians ordered that 12 members of the household should be promptly evicted and the cabin whitewashed. The Primate of all Ireland has issued a letter, referring to the resolution passed by the Archbishops andoßishops, to the effect that a memorial fund should be raised by the Church of Ireland in commemoration of the Jubilee year of her Majesty's reign. In accordance with that resolution he expressed a hope that no decision for local action will be taken by the members of the Church in reference to that matter until the General Synod had de- cided what shape the memorial should take. Mr. John Dillon. M.P., has commenced an action in the Common Pleas Division, Ireland, against County Inspec- tor John Mark O'Brien and District Inspector Hugh ; Davis, to recover £2OOO damages for malicious prosecu- tion and assault, and £l,OOO for the seizure and deten- tion of certain monies, books, and documents. The action arises out of the recent arrest of Mr. Dillon, Mr. O'Brien, and others, at Loughrea, where a rent office was being held in accordance with the "Plan of Campaign." The plaintiff also seeks an order compelling the defendants to deliver up the money, books, and documents seized. Some rather remarkable proceedings are reported as having occurred on the estate of Lord Dillon, in county, Mayo. Lord Dillon, after resisting an abatement of 26 per cent., and after more than 400 ejectment processes and writs for rent had been issued in consequence of the adoption by the tenants of the "plan of campaign," i has, it s reported, granted a reduction of 20 per cent. DRENE.— For lasing drunk and disorderly at Halton, CONFLICT WITH THE POLICE. on the 18th December, Samuel Finch was fined 10s and A prohibited meeting at Roslea, county Fermanagh, costs. was the scene of some exciting incidents on Monday. Mr. en Dillon, M.P., attended, and did his best to outwit the police, and probably if there had been a little more time to alter the original arrangements after the issue of the proclamation, the attempt to hold a meeting would pro- bably have been more successful. As it was, although one or two small meetings were held in the-neighbour- hood, no meeting was permitted and no speeches were delivered in Reales itself, where the great bulk of the people assembled. Mr. Dillon and several Roman Catholic clergymen arrived about two o'clock, and took up their quarters in the village hotel. Here the people, numbering some thousands, collected and cheered. The police prohibited them from massing themselves, how- ever, at this spot, and did their best good-humouredly to prevent them from doing so. They succeeded for a. time, but at length the crowd marched down in a compact body, cheering and shouting and waving blackthorn sticks above their heads. Their intention could be no longer. doubted. They were going to take the space in front, of the hotel. The street is slightly curved, and the crowd were close on the police standing at the hotel' before they were observed. The police made a sudder. effort to close up in front, but before they could do se they were swept away by the crowd, who, with a loud. cheer, massed themselves in the very spot from which the police had been most anxious to exclude them. They stood for a few seconds cheering and shouting and waving the sticks, some of these being branches of trees, but almost instantly the police, by a side movement, got in towards the door of the hotel, and drawing their' batons, sent the crowds decamping up the street. Mr. Dillon and his friends came out and remonstrated with the police, and then Mr. Dillon advised the people to go home.

_ RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. TIP OWD KNOCKER-UP ! Every mornin', i' dark or i' leet, If yor wakken yo'll hear him, aw'm sure; For his clogs onto th' flags cutter-clatter, An' his pow trails behint him on th' floor. He's allus a tag on an' muffler, An' his face Peeps below a black cap When he comes—just at five every mornin'- -. Wl' his tappety, tippety-tap ! He's reglar booath Winter an' Summer— Certain l' dayleet or dark! His pow end fair patters on th' window, ' An' rouses me up to mi wark. Hey, often, when th' thild.er's bin poorly, he aw've settled deawn for th' fost nap, Then aw've thovet him a heartless owd tyrant, Wl' his tappety, tippety-tap ! His yure, its just life frosted silver, He's a nooase like a carrot—breet i•ed ; An' a knot in his gallus, thro' labour; But a steadier mon nooan con ged ! Aw kornd say a wrong word abeawt him, He's a limbersome gammy owd chap, An' he bawls eawt " Ged up !" bowd an' hearty, As he dittheis his tippety-tap ! Aw've wondered at times heaw he does hi; Is his Sleep ruled bi th' stars, or bi th' moon? Aw'm sure, aw' like him, cud ne'er manage To beawnce eawt fro' th' blankets so soon! Aw'll bet as his age is o'er sixty! He mun ha' nailed Time in a trap, For he's sharp as a single young fella, Wl' his tappety-tippety-tap. But aw played him a trick; *when th' top quarrel Up stairs bed bin smashed wi' a bo, Aw wur up th' mornin after, an' waitin' For him on his usual cb ; Be coom, an aw sent sum glass rattlin', Afooar he cud gie th' sekkond slap, An' sheawted " Yo've dominoed th' window Wi' yor tappety-tippety-tap!" He paid me two qhillin' for th' window, An' at parting, he looked sum aft' deawn ! • But aw give id th' owd mon Lack at Kesmas, An' med id i' just hawf-a-creawn! • Aw hope as he'll last o'er a hundred Afooar he sees th' end o' Life's map; An' scatter his cares, just like th' silence, WP his tappety-tippety-tap! Cal tain Plunkett, resident magistrate in Kerry, was called, and examined by Mr. Sullivan. He could not say whether there had been a great deal of agrarian crime in Kerry. It did not occur to his mind, but he could give statistics if he were in his office. He never interfered be- tween landlord-and tenant to the extent of putting pressure upon landlords to.prevent evictions. He admitted that he visited one firm of land agents in Dublin, and sug- gested that one year's rent should be accepted from a tenant. His object was, if possible, to prevent eviction. During the -whole of his five years' experience in Cork and Kerry, he only knew of one harsh landlord. In his opinion, there was no connection between evictions and crime.

Cross-examined by Mr. O'Riordan : He declined to say what passed between him and General Buller, when the latter succeeded him in Kerry. Mr. Walter Scott's latest issue of " The Canterbury Poets" is a volume of the "Sonnets of Europe.' They comprise the best translations of all the great masters of the Sonnet, so that it will be understood that the dainty volume includes not a little of the beet verse that the world has ever known. The sonnets are "selected and arranged with notes" by Mr. Samuel Waddington, himself a sonneteer of no mean order. We have in this delightful collection Italian, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Swedish, Polish, Greek, Dutch, and Latin sonnets—with notes that in themselves are worth more to the general reader than the sum (is.) at which the volume is published.

During Tuesday. it was announced that Sir Henry Hol- land had positively been offered and had accepted the posi- tion of Secretary of State for the Colonies. The post of Vice-President of the Council thus vacated will, it is un- derstood. be offered either to Sir John Horst, Under Secre- tary for India, or Sir Matthew White Ridley, M.P. The acceptance of this office will involve the neceesity of re- election, but in Ministerial circles both Sir John Gurst and Sir Matthew White Ridley are believed to have perfectly safe seats. The sudden death of Lord Iddesleigh •n Wed- nesday, unhappily, settled all controversy as to whether he would have a place in the Ministry. THE RE-ARRANGED CABINET. The following is the composition of the re-arranged Cabinet :
Prime lemisier and Secretary of State for -Foreign Affairs : Marquis of Salisbury. That Lord of the Treasury and Leader of the Eons° of Commons: Mr. WI H. Smith.

The Lord Chancellor: Lord Halsbury. Lord President ot the Council: Viscount Cranbrook. Secretary- of State for Home Affairs: Mr. H. Matthews. Secretary of State for the Colonies: Sir Henry Holland. Secretary of State for War: Mr. E. Stanhope. Secretary of State for India: Viscount Cross. Chancellor of the Exchequer: Mr. G. J. Geschen. First Lord of the Admiralty: Lord George Hamilton. President of the Board of Trade: Lord Stanley. Lord Chancellor of Ireland: Lord Ashtrurne. Chief Secretary for Ireland: Sir M. Hicks-Beech. Secretary of State for Scotland: Mr. A. J. Balfour. Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster: Lord John

At the Colonial Office, on Wednesday, Mr. Stanhope, late Secretary of State for the Coleniee, received the congratula- tions of the Colonial Agents-General on his appointment to the post of Secretary for War. Mr. Goschen en Wednesday issued his address t 3 the electors of the Exchange division of Liverpool. In the pro- posal to establish a separate legislature in Ireland be sees not only disaster to both countries, but an abandonment of national duty. Nothing has occurred within the past six months, he says, to weaken that conviction, but much has occurred to strengthen it. The majority of Englishmen will be less willing than ever to surrender any portion of the United Kingdom to be governed by the advocates of the plan of campaign. The Separatist party, he adols, delude themselves with the idea that surrender to sedition in Ire- land will secire traequility in Great Britain, and a peace- ful era of beneficient legislative ectivity. Such a surrender will, in his opinion, be the first Atop in a downward course ef national disintegration and decay. Mr. Neville, the Liberal candidate for Liverpool, attended at the committee rooms, 47, St. Ann-street, on Wednesday evening, and addressed the canvassers from the ward asso- ciation and from the City Reform Club. LORD R. CHURCHILL--IMPORTANT LETTERS The following correspondence has been forwarded for publication :--- risses Office, Wallingford, Jan. Bth, 1887. My Lord,— I have the honour to inform you that, at a meeting of the St.. Stephen's (Wallingford) Habitation of the Prim- rime League, held on the 6th instant, the following amendment to a resolution was carried by a very large majority i--0 That this meeting deeply regrets the resignation of Lord Randolph Churchill, but remembers, with gratitude, the great services he has rendered to the Tory cause, and sincerely hopes he will continue to show his warm interest in the Conservative working men of this country." • Your lordship may be interested to learn that this amendment, proposed by myself and seconded by my co-steward, Mr. W. Park, received the support of all the working men present, who separated with a hearty cheer for "Lord Randolph."—Yours respectfully . (Signed), T. Witsom. 2, Connaught-place, W., Jan. 10th, 1887. My dear desire to express to you my deep- gratification with the communication which you have made to me. The working men of Wallingford have. ; certainly' shown themselves to be more generous and • reserved in their political judgment than many Conser- vative members of Parliament, who have been prompt, not to say precipitate, in pronouncing unqualified con- demnation on my recent action, although, as regards the nature and causes of that action, they are almost entirely without information. I am not without some amount of confidence that when that action becomes a matter of public personal explanation, the opportunity for which, at the present moment, is rigorously denied to me, much ,of the hasty adverse criticism may be modified, but, 'whether that is so or not I care little. The approval of • such persons as I allude to is as worthless an article as. their disapproval. lam perfectly and fully conscious of having sought for nothing but the public interest, and: I have also a very considerable expectation that before long the public interest will by no means suffer from the increased activity of criticism which Parliament may be tempted to bestow on the proposals of the Executive as. regards finance and expendittrre.—l am, yours faithfully, (Signed), • fflornoten S. Clitracmtt. T. Wilson, Esq. Writing to a Bradford Correspondent, on Monday, Mr. Gladstone expressed the opinion that Lord Randolph Churchill resigned upon justifiable grounds. Mr. Glad- stone says that he is in favour of more economy being exercised, both in regard to the army and the navy. He wishes to refrain, however, from committing himself in any way on the point whether the present condition of the navy and the coaling stations demand increased. 1-expenditure. 1, Lord R. Churchill proposes to 'leave England for the Continent in the course of this week. His explanation' ,in Parliament will he made after arrangement with the Government, and when the production of the corre- spondence between himself and Load Salisbury can take 1 place without prejudice to the interests of the party. 'Lord R_ Churchill will be in no hurry to state his reasons for resigning, and his explanations will give rise to no leach scenes as occurred on the secession of the Liberal • !Unionists. His will be explanations without recrimina- • tions.-7Leadois Correspondent INAUGURATING A RETRENCHMENT POLICY. The War Estimates for the coming year are aeain to I be revised by the heads of departments before they are, submitted to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the. greatest care is to be taken that everything that is not absolutely Accessary and indispensable to the safety or the empire is eliminated. " Both Lord Salisbury and the • Chancellor of the Exchequer have written to the, Treasury, pointing out that the ievenue is not air elastic as it was, and that there is every sign of an ever- increasing taxation. The income-tax has risen from 21.. to Bd. during the last ten years, and represents an annual income of £12,000,000. The Treasury ' are told to write to all the Government departments urging a closer scrutiny on the part of the head officials' into the estimates which are brought forward by their juniors, and no fresh expense is to be incurred without. I the fullest evidence that the non-compliance with the, demand would be a positive danger to the State. Great ' stress is laid on the point of not increasing the staff of . clerks in the departments, and we tray expect, that a reduction and rearrangement of the personnel will follow the various inquiries now going on. The Government expect a rather. j stormy time in the coming session as to the imoney which will be required for the army and nary' and other spending departments. In view of this the bon. members at the head of affairs are being supplied "with all information necessary to meet the crop of inquiries and criticisms which they expect.. The state of the revenue and of taxation 10 years ,ago and their position now are to be compared,and all the causes • -which have conspired to bring in such heavy-budgets are being carefully collaborated. We may shortly expect,; therefore, to hear some very interesting debates on the, subject of how we stand with regard to finance, and our army and navy.

RAILWAY EstpLorEs DINNEEL—The first of the annual dinners given by manufacturers and colliery proprietors in St. Helens and surrounding districts to the brakemen, shunters, signalmen, ecc., employed during the year on the various sidings connecting the works with the London and North-Western Railway Company, took place at the Rail- way Inn, Sutton. About forty persons sat down to a sub- stantial repast, after which Mr. Lucas, stationmaster at St. Helens Junction, and Mr. Leather, stationmaster at Sutton Oak, occupied the chair and vice-chair respectively. The "Health of the Queen,!' with special reference to her Majesty's jubilee, was given and heartily responded to. This was followed by "The Town and Trade of St. Helens" " The Donors," "The London and North-Western Railway Company," and "The Press." The proceedings were inter- spersed with songs, recitations, &o. THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE AND THE IMPERIAL INSTITUTE.—A large meeting was held on Wednesday in the Mansion House to further a national memorial of Her Majesty's Jubilee. Lord Granville moved a resolution urging voluntary effcrt. This was carried, together with one proposed by Mr. Goschen approving of its taking the form of an Imperial Institute under the direction of the Prince of Wales. A largely-attended meeting in support of a scheme for an Im- perial Institute of the United Kingdom, the Colonies, and India was held on Wednesday, at 6t. Jame's Palace, the Prince of Wales presiding. His Royal Highness said the desire to find the means of uniting the colonies and India in closer bonds with the mother country met with tpe Queen's warmest sympathy. He proposed that the Imperial Institute should be the emblem of the unity of the Empire and illustrate the resources and capabilities of the Empire. On the motion of Earl Spencer, seconded by the Lord Provost of Edinburgh, a resolution was carried that the foundation of an Imperial Institute would be fitting to commemorate the completion of the fiftieth year of the Queen's reign. It was also resolved on the motion of Lord Hampden, seconded by the Lord Mayor of York that an appeal be made to all the subjects of the Queen for support te the rriheme. A. vote of thanks to the Prince of Wales concluded the proceedings.

"In Letters of flame" is the title of a new novel, in one volume, published by Messrs. Cassell and Co. It is from the pen of C. L. Mateanx, author of " ave Lives and Noble," "Round About Old Eng- land," &o. "In Letters of Flame" is stale of the Waldenses; and, as may be supposed, it is of excit- ing interest. Yet it cannot be said to be sensational either in plot or incident, the dramatic element be- ing the simple and natural outcome of the extraor- dinary circumstances of the time. The chief charac- ters of the story are drawn with singular firmness and clearness. The Student Bazile, who sets himself the task of going from amongst the simple mountaineers to acquire learning at the university of Paris in order that he may fight by 'pen and tongue for the Re- formed Church, is a oareful study. How love proves the master motive, and bow it leads him for atime out of the path he had selected for loimeelt is beautifully told. The woman he has chosen to be his wife is a I devout Catholic, who is horror struck when she even- tually learns that her husband is a Reformee ; and nothing can exceed the pathos of the parting of the two—except, let us add, the touching scene of their re-union. The author gives a graphic picture of the , manners and customs of the period; and, although the book reveals the failings of the Catholic Church, I there is nothing of sectarian bitterness in its tone. I Persecution in dealt with rather as a matter of his- tory than with a desire to make out a case. The style is marked by a sabtle vein of humour which is exceed- ingly characteristic and very agreeable. "In Letters of Flame" takes high rank as an historioal novel ; it , can be read by all classes with interest and profit. " The Romance of Invention; Vignettes from the Annals of Industry and Science," by James Burnley, author of "Two Sides of the Atlantic," &c. This im- portant work from the prom of Messrs. Cassell and Co., is likely to meet with a good reception from the public and prove of abiding interest. No one who is familiar with the lives of inventors can fail to have been struck vrith the romantic way in which some of the most important discoveries have been made; and it is therefore a happy thought and a useful thing to bring the "Romance of Invention" within the scope of a goodly volume of nearly eoo pages. As the author frankly remarks, "there Ass necessarily been a large extent of literary labour laid under cosakri- , button in the bringing together of so many facts, but the main sources of information have been indicated in the text. Although his research has extended into many odd nooks and °omen, no trustworthy source has been ignored; and here and there his own know- ledge or industry has brought into prominence facts which have not before been dealt with, and which will, he believes, make the narrative more valuable." The following are some of the topics treated upon in the twenty-four chapters into which the book is di- vided :—the beginniegs of invention, martyrs of in- vention, inventions in poetry and fiction, iaventors in love, through poverty and suffering, royal and noble inventors, costly machinery, inventors in toyland, on the sea, and amongst the wires, inventions discovered by accident, revolutions of wheelland, machinery riots, inventors in the battlefield, in bookland, &c. The work is suitably illustrated by Gordon Brown, who has taken as his subjects :—the be. sighted farm labourer in Huntsman's foundry, Queen Elizabeth's visit to William Lee, Senefelder and the washerwoman's bill, Vaucanson's tiuteplayer, Prince Rupert and the scldier, and Frederick the Great and the sentinel Jew's harpist. The book is handsomely bound, the cover being enriched by an illustration of the famous incident of Watt watching the kettle on the kitchen fire. There is a copious index for refer- ence purposes ; and, as Mr. Burnley has throughout done his work well, "The Romance of Invention " is all that could be desired. " Cassell's Illustrated Shakespeare," part 12, com- mences The Metchant of Venice." The full page illustrations are very striking, and it is a matter of course to say that " Shylock is a prominent figure in them. The notes by Charles and Mary Cowden Clarke are highly inetructive to the sttichint of the I language of which the great bard was such a great , master. But for precise and exhaustive knowledge in this respect one cannot do better than turn to "The Eneyolopcedio Dictionary," which embraces all the words in the English language, with a full account of their origin; meaning, pronounciation, history, and use. Part 36 to hand is a continuation of the letter G, and brings the thied volume to a close. Part 35 of "The Book of Health" deals with climate and health resorts; and puts the invalid who has means in a posi- tion to know to a nicety how various parts of the world would be likely to affect his condition.

Part 17 of Cassell's "Gleanings from Popular Authors" sustains the high reputation of the work alike as io selections and illustrations. When com- plete the volume will be one that will be a favourite In every household. Part ii of "Familiar wild Flowers" is adorned with full page coloured plates of the germander speedwell and the ox-eye daisy, and it is needless to say to those who are familiar with pre. 'vious parts that they are finished in the highest style of art. The text, if all too brief, is a good summary of what is known of the flowers. "The Life and Times of Queen Victoria" is naturally in great demand for the Jubilee Year of Her Majesty's reign. The illustrations are remarkable alike for their num- ber and beauty. Part 8 covers the years 1850-51•52. "Wanderings in South America," by Charles Water- ton, is the latest issue in the National Library series, published at 3d each. We have also to hand " Cas-i sell's Illustrated Catalogue," which is a work of art in itself, besides being useird for reference as to the numerous books issued by this onterptising firm. The frontispiece is a picture of the balcony scene from "Romeo and Juliet ; " it is quite a revelation as to the beauty and delicacy of the photogravure process. We have recently had occasion to notice the merits of " Cassell's Magazine," and for further details we have pleasure in directing the reader to an advertise- inent in another part of the paper. "The Bianctister Quarterly 'S is a journal of litera- ture and art published by Mi. John Heywood, Man- chester and London. The number for January con-, tame some interesting papers, the first place being deservedly given to "An Impression of Niagara," by Mr. Thomas Kay. It is thoughtfully and tastefully written; and is accompanied by a most artistic illus- tration by the author. Two carefully prepared maps support an article on the "Common Field System in and near Manchester," by Mr. H. T. Crofton. Mr. John Mortimer gossips pleasantly on "December Daisies;" and the Rev. W. A. O'Conor contributes a paper on "The Paetry of the Bible," which will bear reading a second time. Sir James A. Baton treats on the ancient commercial relations of Chester and Liver- pool; and "Literature and Politics" are dealt with in "A Christmas Symposium." We have also to hand from Mr- Heywood part 3 of the new and extended edition of "Baines's History of Lancashire." It gives a history of the Duchy of Lancaster, of which one hears chiefly when the Ministerial appointment is made. It may be noted that Sir Henry de Haydok 'was the first Chancellor of the Duchy, in `1360. Mr. Goechen was Chancellor in 1866, and Mr. John Bright has been twice Chancellor—in 1873 and in 1880,, The present Chancellor is Lord John Manners. The 'office pf Sheriff of Lancashire dates back to Iz7S, when the post was held by Ralph Fitz-Bernard. Col. MoCor- quodale was Sheriff in 1882, and the presentholder of the office is Sir A. B. Walker.

" The Moon Maiden and other stories" by Jessy E. I Greenwood, is a charming book for the little folk, pub- lished by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It is a fairy tale of the adventures of a pretty princess who came down from the moon to share the troubles and trials of the people of this world. Dan, the hero, is very heroic indeed, and it is no wonder, after doing so many good and brave deeds, that he is permitted to go to the moon with the princess, where, of course, they both" live happy ever after." ;" Sposin "is the title of one of the shorter stories, but it is decidedly the best; for it is throughout coherent and artistic. " Sposin" is a fairy who believes in work- ing as well as dreaming, and has great rewards for those who stick to a task they have once set them- selves to eo. "Prince Jasmine" will captivate the boys as being full of adventure of a truly marvellous kind. The author has a special gift of fancy in this class of stories. She can entertain the youthful, and teach them something in the way of a moral lesson without letting them know they are being taught. The volume, it should be added, is nicely bound,and it is a model cf good printing. " Great Writers" is the title of a series of shilling , volumes to be issued monthly by Mr. Walter Scott, London. The first is the Life of Henry Wads- worth Longfellow," by Mr. Eric S. Robertson, M.A. In addition to furnishing a very interesting and reli- able record of the career of the great American poet, there is a fine critical estimate of his genius; and a valuable "Bibliography," prepared by Mr. J. P. An- derson. As the volnme is well bound and well prin- ted, there should be a great demand for it; it is ab- surdly cheap.

wile Letters and Journals of Lord Byron (selected) constitute the January volume of the Camelot Classics' published by the same firm. The introduction, by 31athilde Blind, is thoughtfully and sympathetically written. After a generation of Byron worship there was a reaction against him; and it is about time now to get a just estimate of his place and power. The .t.etters help to show Byron as he was--a being of great parts and great passions with the "strength to dare, to defy, and to do.' They are as readable as anything the poet has written, and that

WIDNES RECREATION V WIDNES Sr. MARY'S (CATUO• Lic.)—The Rees journeyed to Millfield on Saturday, to play eff the West Lancashire Junior Cup Tie, but to the disap- pointment of the assembled footballers the appointed referee, Mr. Dean, of Rancorn, failed to make his appear- ance, and consequently the Cup Tie bad to be abandoned. After a discussion of considerable length, the respective captains agreed to play a match for the gate, which turned out an exciting and pleasant game under the circumstances. The Reos. were severely handicapped by the absence of Grundy, Bradshaw, and Sumner, while their opponents put on their full strength. Roouey kicked off with the wind, the ball being returned into the home quarters where after a series of scrimmages the Recs, forwards dribbled well, and suc- eeeded in taking the ball over the line, but failed to ground it. From the drop-out the visitors con- tinued to show their superiority, their combined play show. ing to great advantage, Broome, Ritnmer, Flynn, and Bran- son being most conspicuous. The Saints then reused themselves to their best ability, and carried play into the Rece 25, where it remained at half-time, the Rees haying a minor point to their credit. On re-starting the Rees were bent oa victory, and twain their forwards carried the play I Into the home territory, but Meagher and Hewitt came to the rescue and transferred the play into mid-field. Give. and-take Play was now indulged in, until Rtrnmer passed well to Broome, who punted up the field. McCririe and Flynn following up with great dexterity, after a lengthy dribble, crowned their efforts by a splendid try, the kick at r goal failing. Nothing of importance occurred up to the call of time, although it may be mentioned that the home team had to defend their lines well to prevent the smart " juven- iles" from scoring, the score being, Recreation, one try and two minor points to nil. It would be invidious to criticize the play of the winners, but the pick of the Saints were Brennan, Doyle, Donohue, Rooney, and Hewitt. Referee. Mr. W. Hartley, Widnes. WARRINGION V. SALFORD (lsr TEAMS,) The meeting of these two teams, holding, as they both do, prominent places in the front rank of Lancashire Rugby Clubs was looked forward to with great interest in War- rington. The weather having recently been so thoroughly of a wintery character fears were felt that the match would be prevented like that of the previous week, but fortunately a thaw having set in every effort was made by the execu- tive of the Warrington Football Club to add to its effect. The ground was cleared of snow, and large fires were kept on the ground to soften it on Friday night. The result was that when the Salford team arrived at Warrington, and their captain having visited the ground, it was decided to play off the fixture. There were over 3,000 spectators present, but there can be little doubt that this number would have been doubled had the weather been of a more favourable character.

Salford won the toss, and two 25's being the time agreed upon, Frank Turner kicked off at 3 5, and Ashton, following well up, charged Buxton's kick down, the ball going into touch at the Salford quarter flag. From the line out Fair. Turner passed to Barnes, who kicked to Mainwaring, but Rigby was on him before he could get away, a free kick be- ing conceded. Massey returned the ball to Salford 25, where the Warrington forwards carried the scrimmage, and Gilbert getting bold passed to Barnes, who punted to Main- waring, and this player kicked into touch. Salford now touched down in cell-defence, amid much cheering from the spectators. Ottiwell dropped out, and Jolley returned to G. Buxton, Frank Turner and that player coming into collis- ion. Buxton retired, and his brother Charles took his place at half-back. Williams relieved, but Gilbert saved nicely. Dillon, Littlewood, and Ashton here came through the scrimmage* Littlewood collaring Mainwaring with the oval. Eagles and Shaw gained a little ground, but Massey kicked to the visiting full beck, who touched down. Slater dropped out, and Barnes receiving the ball made a good run and kick, but Stott, Barlow, and Shaw rushed the leather to cen- tre, where Fairfield Turner gained possession and made a grand run, only being brought down about a yard from the line. From the scrimmage which followed, Gilbert passed to Barnes, who dropped a splendid goal amid intense excitement. Ottiwell reatarted, and Fair Turner ran the ball back, a scrimmage being formed near the centre. Walmeley now took a flying kick, Povey recovering the lost ground. Some good kicking between Barnes and Mainwaring was now witneased,the ball resting in neutral ground. C. Buxton here saved a danger- ous rush. Speakman next made a grand dribble, but Slater came to the rescue of his side. Williams, Eagles, and Roberts got away, but Jolley saved, and C. Buxton pressed on further, but Barnes kickgei into touch. Some passing between the visiting forwards rook place at this period, Var. ley at last gaining possession, bat Jolley was too many for him. Massey and Barnes were next prominent in a good dribble, taking the ball to the Salford 25, and collared Malliwaring with the leather. Eagles broke away, Speak. ma bringing him down nicely. Frank Turner here dribbled the oval to the Salford line,Walmaley kicking dead. ' Slater dropped out,and following well up, collared Barnes before he could return. The Salford forwards gained further ground, but Dillon and Hayes ran the oval back. Walmsley now got,hold, and made a good run, Barnes pushing him into touch. Rigby, Dillon, Fair. Turner, and Hayes carried the next scrfmmage, the former running the.ball to the grand stand, where Buxton saved. This brought about half time, the score standing—Warringion, 1 goal and 4 minors, to Salford uil. Ottiwell re-started, and Fair. Turner returned to Walmsley, who punted to Barnes, this player returning to Walmsley, whom Ashton collared before he could get his kick in, the oval resting in the Salford quarters. Williams, Shaw, and Stott broke away, dribbling to Appleton, who kicked into touch. Ashton, Dillon, and Povey retaliated, but Eagles removed play to the Warrington 25, where Speakman saved finely. Some tall kicking between Slater and Jolley now took place, and immediately afterwards Appleton was allowed a free kick for off-side play. Davies was next to show up in a neat dribble, play resting in Sal- ford •quarters. Speakman here got clear away, and punted to Walmaley, who returned into touch in centre. Williams, Barlow, and Roberts removed play to the home 25, but the brothers Turner. Povey, and Littlewood rushed the oval back again. Barnes now obtained possession in neutral ground, and dodging through the thick of his opponents made the best run of the day, and finished up by passing to Frank Turner,a scrimmage being formed near the visitors' goal line. Eagles and Barlow removed the pressure, and Apple- ton kicked into touch. Ottiwell broke away, but Hayes brought him down. Clegg further improved matters for Salford, rushisg the oval to the home quarter flag. Fair. Turner, Rigby. and Mks dribbled to centre, but Williams brought the ball back, Barnes saving by dropping on the ball in front of the stand. Povey, Davies, Littlewood, and Ashton ran the oval to the visitors' 25, Slater being called upon to save. Oa the leather becoming loose Varley tried to kick dead about 15 yards from the line, but Frank Turner rushing up dropped on the ball and claimed a try, but the referee would not allow the point, and only a minor was registered. After the drop out Barnes was prominent with a grand dribble, and Varley getting hold panted to Jolley, who returned to Salford 25. Williams here put in a splendid dribble to the home quarter flag, and shortly after- wards Massey ran back to touch down, this being the visitors' first point. Frank Turner re-started, and Povey collared Eagles before he could part with the oval. Smith and Shaw broke away from the scrimmage, and Gilbert saved nicely. Clegg here passed to Varley, who punted, but Jolley and Barnes recovered the loot ground. Verbs] again obtained possession and gained a lot of ground, but lost the ball, and Davies saved. Varley next had a drop at goal, and Appleton failing to hold the leather, Massey kicked dead. Frank Turner dropped out and Clegg ob- tained a free kick, Slater taking the place, but Ashton charged the kick down. Shortly afterwards time wash called, leaving Warrington victors by 1 goal and 4 minors I to Salfoid 2 minors.

The game throughout was distinguished by heavy for. Ward play. The Salford team, it is well known, are strong in this department, but on the present occasion it was soon seen that they had met their equals, and on the whole the home team had the best of the sciimmages. In the case of the Warrington forwards It is difficult to particularize where all did so well in their various ways. Fair Turner was as usual very conspicuous, and in this match be was seen at his very best ; Ashton, the captain, likewise did I some smart work, as did Dillon, Davies, Frank Turner, Hayes and Rigby. The nalf.backs, Gilbert and Speakman, it is hardly needful to say, both did well, Gilbert on several occasions showing fine judgment, and Speakman playing when necessary a pluck" defensive game. The trio of , three-quarters were in their best form. Barnes, incited, i

almost excelled himself, and, to say nothing of his kicking ' the winning point, on numberless occasions he showed him- self to be more than a match tor his opponents Appleton ' is doing well at back, and though his play on Saturday was not altogether without blemish, he more than once dis- played excellent judgment and quickness in warding off danger. The visitors one and all played in a style worthy of their reputation, and especially towards the end of the game. Among the forwards Eagles, Shaw, and Williams were prominent, and amongst the backs, Walmsley, Slater, and Clegg. Teams :—Salford : Fall back, Mainwaring; three-quarter backs, Walmsley, Valley (captain), and Slater; half backs, Clegg and G Buxton ; forwards, Eagles, Williams, Stott, Barlow, Smith, Roberts, Ottiwell, Heald, and Shaw. War- rington: Full back, Appleton; three-quarter backs, Massey, Barnes, and Jolley; ball backs, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, Fair. Turner, Ashton (captain), Dillon, EigbY, Hayes, Frank Turner, Davies, Povey, and Littlewood. Um- pires, Messrs Vickers and Barnes; referee, Mr Lord, Broughton P.C.

There are not a few persons woo do not hesitate to say that the larger part of the high-gn" talk about the celebration of the jubilee year is itifit much sound, and will "signify nothing" so far as an 7 tangible or permanent outcome is concerned, and there 13 ; not a little to countenance this prediction. The jubile°_,YZ has come, and it is rapidly gliding on its way, and when we look round we see that, locally, nothing has s'!_, been authoritatively taken in hand to signalise it. It "Imo° I be an ignoble conclusion to all the fine talk that was dulged in by leading people in Warrington when the labile! ' year was still in prospect if, after all, nothing is done. Ana of all places such a result would be inexcusable inWarrinif- ton, where the work of freeing the library lies at band be done. Patmor.—These clubs met at Pros- oot on Saturday in the presence of several hundreds of spec- tators, and although the snow was several inches deep, a splendid game was witnessed. The visitors had the best of Lb. play, and ran out winners of a well-fought game by seven goals to one. The visitors all played a fine consistent game throughout, whilet for the losers Stott Knox and Lyon played excellently. Prescot— THE MOLOCH OF FARAFFIN. Cookson, goal ; Lyon and Whitfield, backs; Knox, Mere- Slr,—ln glancing over a file of your valuable DaPer dith, and Case (captain), half backs; Stott, Woods, Henry 'notice that you recently called attention in powerful 130' Welaby, and Walker, forwards.guage to Mr. Marvin's pamphlet on paraffin lamp accidents. lam at the present moment detained from home by the I consequences of one of these frightful disasters; and the enforced leisure, and my painfully increased interest in the subject, have led me to certain conclusierns, of which I all anxious to express one or two in connection with your avid remarks. You quote Mr. Marvin's assertion that one an only one lamp at present made gives complete immunity from danger; and you follow it with his appeal for Perlis; mentary interference. I feel so strongly the urgent nee' for legislation on the subject, and see so clearly the ear with which a quite workable provision could be made 10, the Petroleum Bill, that I venture te express my earnes‘ hope that the sequence in year notice does not imply a ear gestion that legislation should interfere in favour of a Par; ticular safety lamp. The enormous importance whic should be attached to our cheapest form of illumination, will, and should stop any attempt to place the sale in the hands of a single firm, however enterprising. The fir!t condition of safety is that breakable reservoirs should w_ absolutely forbidden. Now herein lies the great difficult° of the problem. Breakable reservoirs are the great Cant as lamps are made at present, of the accidents. But it ‘l,l obvious that breakable reservoirs are a regular source profit to maker and seller of lamps who has to renew the So no state of affairs in which breakable reservoirs wer I abolished would meet with the approval of the lamp trade. ' They have indeed raised with justice one argument againet s such a step. They say that metal reservoirs, raising Ih , eil to a higher temperature, renders explosion more 11101'; This Is very true, so long as the present types of burner a used. But if we were to insist that the wick-tube well brought nearly to the bottom of the metal reservoir, an; all communication between flame and reservoir prohibit except through the wick, we sheuld have a lamp in evert respect safe, and open to be made in every shop In the king; dom. As no vapour could escape, it would not matter ho much was generated, and the quality of oil used woula_ therefore be a matter of indifference. A provision such 53 this would be free from the objection which attaches te any monopoly, would inflict no needless hardship on WI makers, and would effectually protect the masses from tu, ravages of the Moloch of Paraffin. The public, ignorant ir technicalities, are in the hands of the trade ; and the trade of their own motion will naturally not stir. Is it not tan° that, with the yearly increase in the number of these acct . dents and the calamities which arise ariee from them, Fsr. liament should step in and prevent the wholesale slaughtat of life and destruction of property which the license 110' granted to lamp manufacturers involves?
