NOTES BY THE WAY. Our readers will be glad to hear that Tad Warren is again going to don the primrose and blue on Saturday next with the Warrington A team, at Hulme, Manchester. The players from the iron town of Barrow-in-Furness bay a visit to-day and, according to form, should play a good game, and one which will be a treat to the Warrington spectators, being a flue open one. But still the odds are that Ashton's lads will prove the victors, although the Barrovians will be a hard nut to crack. Dewsbury are having a tour in Easter week, and wish to take on Warrington on the Thursday, having sent a chal- lenge to that effect; but it is not likely that the match will take place on account of Warrington playing on the Friday, Saturday, and Monday. This, however, shows that the best clubs of Yorkshire, as well as Lancashire, do not think it any disgrace to play against the best club of West Lancashire. In local football circles the defeat of Salford by Warring- ton has naturally been regarded as a "glorious victory." The Rugby premiership of Lancashire has been declared on authority to lie between Salford reed Swinton, but after the recent performance of Warrington it is evident that this club will have to be reckoned with. The match on Saturday Wile a very fair teat of the merits of the two teams, for although the ground was net everything that could be desired this told as much against one lot as the other. There could .be no doubt in the minds of those who witnessed the march that Salford did everything they could to uphold their colours, and it was by nothing but sheer downright good play that the home team notched their victory. Everybody was glad to see Ashton again at the head of Warrington players on Saturday, and It was soon seen that from a footballing point of view his recent illness had left no traces behind, for he never played in better style than on Saturday. With regard to other players, it is now fully expected that after their achievement last week Barnes and Fairfield Turner will be invited to do duty in tne county team. It will be rather strange if they are not. At the meeting of the Executive of the West Lancas- hire and Border Towns Rugby Union held on Tuesday ' evening, the draws were ma 'e for the first round of the Competition for the challenge cup, won last year by the Warrington team, with the following result :—Tuebrook V Tyldesley, Liverpool Wanderers v Walton, St. Helena v Warrington, Widues v Blaekrod, Walkden v Leigh, Bootle v St. Helens Recreation, Litherland v Wigan, Aspull • Southport Olympic. It will be seen that St Helens and Warrington will meet in the first round this year, and as the club whose name is mentioned first has the choice of ground in each case, the St. Helens club will have the privilege of deciding where the encounter is to take place. At the same meeting it was mentioned that the following matches were still to be played in connection with the junior competition : Warrington St. Paul's v Lyerim, Newton v Farnworth, St Mary's (Widnes) v Widnes Recrea- tion, Pemterton v Lowe House Tree Blues, Wigan Rovers v Highfield, New Brighton Olympic v Blundelleands, and Waterloo St. John's v Edge-hill. It was ordered that these matches were to be completed to-day (Saturday.) In con- nection with this competition the following draws were also made for the second round :—Warrington Hornets V St. Cleopas, St. James (Wigan) v Widnes Recreation or St Mary's, Scot-lane v Edge-hill or Waterloo St Johns, Run- corn Recreation v Lowe House True Blues or Pemberton, Bedford (Leigh)v Sutton, Wigan Rovers or Hightield Lymm or St Paul's, Standish South End v Birkenhead Wanderers, Farnwerth or Newton v New Brighton Olympic or Blundellsands, 4th L.A.V. a bye. The ties have to be. played on or befere Saturday, the 22nd inst. The International match between England and Wales was brought off on Saturday at Llanelly before 4n immense gathering of spectator& The ground was not in the best condition but nevertheless a fine and evenly-balanced con- test was the result of the meeting, ending in a draw in favour of Wales by five minors to two miners. The team that represented England was composed of the following players :—S Roberts (Swinton) 'back; R Robertsbaw (Bradford), J Le Fleming , (Cambridge University), and R Lockwood (Dewsbury), three-quatter backs • F Bonsor (Bradford) and A Rotherham (Richmond), *half-backe f•W G Clibborn (Richmond), N fipurling (Blackheath), C R Cleveland (Oxford University), J II Dewburst (Cambridge University), UC Baker (Gloucestershire), E Wilkinson (Bradford), J L Hickson (Bradford), R Seddon (Broughton Rangers), and II Springman (Liverpool) forwards. GOOD THISPLART.—The weekly session of the nopo of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day evening, when there was a fnll attendance, and Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. Two new candidates were proposed, and one new member was initiated, after which fraternal visits to Whiston and Golborne were arranged. The evening's programme was "Mailbag night," and letters of an entertaining character were read from Brother J. W. Hall, D.0.T., Warrington ; Brother J. H. Musk, D.E.S., Manchester; Brother M. Jones, W.D.S., Liverpool ; lire. J. Oliver, W.DAL, Liverpool ; Brother George Clarke, W.D.Coun., Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., Brother J. Bar- nard to his brother in India; and a humorous one signed "Brother Charity's Checaboard." A cordial vote of thanks WAS tendered to the writers of the communications. A selection of songs, recitations, &c., was afterwards given by the members. PERSONS REILIIIIIING LOANS of Li and upwards at the lowest rate of interest, should apply at 7, Wellington. Street, Earlestows.—Adrot.

div.p: WIT 4ND HUMOUR. _ - _

• The only% place in which the average woman can be placed what), she can think of absolutely nothing the wants to say, is at a telephone. A French judge fined a starving man 87 for stealing a loaf of bread, and then paid the fine out of his own pocket. Law and conscience are often opposed to each other. Two DAMAGE.—" Say, they had an awful time down to Jonao' lac.t night." "I haven't heard anything about it." "Yes, the hew caught fire, Jones lost his head, and such a commotion you neyff saw.* "Oh, well it won't take much to reribar the lose," Chief of detective bureau: "you wish employment on the force, eh ? How would you proceed in a delicate interview ?" Applicant: "Oh, I'd skirmish adroitly for awhile; then, when I had Succeeded in arresting his attention, I would—" "That will do, sir. You can consider yourself engaged. Hang me if I don't want a man on my force who can succeed in arresting some- thing or other." A man in Cincinnati has been left seven different legacies by seven different uncles and aunts. Relatives are of some good—once in a great while.. One reason why there are not more marriages in Tennessee is because the young fellow is expected to do his courting in the presence of the old folks. The "great esteem" in which the retiring mayor of an Indiana town was held was shown in the presenta- tion to him, by forty-four leading citizens, of a horse which ran away with him the first day he gob it and broke two of his ribs and a leg. Had they presented him with a set of resolutions he would have 'had no suf- fering and no doctor s bills. SPRING CHICKENS.—" Remember those chickens you sold me Saturday ?" "Certainly." "spring chickens, weren't. they?" "Of course. What was the matter with them?" "Oh, nothing. The springs were all there, only I wanted to tell you that the next time I want a pair with rubber springs. Wire springs are too rich for my blood." PESSIMIST AND OPTlMlST.—Sophronia! "What is a pessimist?" A pessimist is a man who growls when the meat is overdone, growls when it is underdone, growls when it is neither over nor underdone, and can- not see anything good in the world except when he is looking into his mirror. To your other question, "What is an optimist?" we reply that he is a whole- souled, jolly—but call in and see us in person some day; we don't charge anything for being looked at. A WILD WOMAN.—It was on a Madison street car. The driver was fat, red in the face, and solemn. Looking around to the splitary smoker who stood there, he said: "I see that they have found a wild woman down in Pennsylvania." "Yes," replied the smoker, who did not propose to have any ancient gag played on him. The driver riveted his eyes on the horses and maintained profound silence until he had crossed the bridge, when he observed: "But that ain't nothing, mister. You cad see wild women any day on the West Side when the car don't stop in the middle of the block. Git on there, now, will ye?"

div.head: SCHOOL.
div.p: SCHOOL.
WARRINGTON RAGGED SUNDAY -

scarce covered their nakedness, and girls whose clothing was wofully scant; little todillers whose legs dangled from the fprms, and who *ent fast to sleep warmed by the unaccustomed heat, with their heads resting against,their elder brothers and sisters in distress. There were others who sang' lustily the chorus of the • hymn they had learned, and others, again, stood open-eyed and amazed, not yet. understanding what manner of thing had come to pass.. After singing, the child- ren,itneeling, repeated the Lord's Prayer with the superintendent, and it was gratifying to see that not a few of them were converSant with it. Soon afterwards the meeting closed, and the children left 'With the promise to come again next nday. The promise will be kept, and gladly. "One hundred and fifty ragged children!" One would almost wonder where they all came from, but there was no difficulty in gathering them to:. gether. A short walk through some of the streets ,on Sunday week was enough, and last Sunday " missionmg " had to be abandoned, as all the seats so far provided were occupied. Proper accommoda- tion could not have been found for more, and to turn them away would have been cruel. The children are those of the very, poorest class. Many pf their parents by hard Work can scarcely gain a hand-to- mouth living of the most meagre kind for them- selves and families; some are not able to get work at all, and some, alas, belong to that class below— the idle and intemperate. Woeful is the condition of some of these half-famished. children. Some may have homes that are a little like home, but many can scarcely be considered to have a" home" at all, and of some it might almost be quoted, " Homeless near a thousand hornet they stood, and near a thousand tables pined and wanted f00d,7 Surely, in face of a state of things like this a Ragged Sunday School comes as a bleBsmg to them. The children are among u 6 in all their wretchedness and misery, the school has been set in motion and What is now required is that it should be kept in motion. It is not an expensive institution, and is not likely to be. The children are thankful for small mercies, and are not of the sort to prove too exacting. Charity, surely, will not turn a deaf ear to the ap- peal, and the duty too long neglected will be cheer- fully taken up. Those whose own means are but limited, or who have already many claims upon them, can assist by sending cast-off clothing, and in that way they will do great good, while there are scores, nay hundreds, who could give a little monetary assistance towards 69 good an object. They might do very much worse with a spare shill- ing than hand it over to the committee of the War- ruigton Ragged School.

Until the, • commencement of the present year, Warrington, with its large working population, has been without any school for ragged children, al- though most other manufacturing towns of a similar size have not been so neglected. The idea that in this respect Warrington, with all its churches and chapels, charitable movements and in- stitutions, has been behind hand, must often have forced itself on the attention of earnest, thinking men, and the wonder is that something was not done years ago on behalf of the ragged urchins in the town, whose days are spent in the streets, and' whose nights are in many cases passed in homes of wretchedness and squalor. The claims of these little waifs only require thinking of to be admitted; and now that a start has been made in their favour by the establishment of a Ragged Sunday School, aid is required from the benevolent to carry the movement to a successful issue. In the correspon- dence columns of this journal there appeared on the 18th of December last the first intimation that it was intended to form a Ragged School in Warring- ton. In a letter Mr. James Skelland, of 60, Bewsey- road, wrote as follows :—" I have had an impression for years, deepened very much of late, that Ragged Schools are a great want of Warrington, to train the poor children in the way they should g?. At present how many are being trained by their sur- roundings in all kinds of vice and sin? At the Silver-street Mission services on Sunday evenings it is heartrendinglo see so many half-clad children glad to get out of the rain and cold, and it is inter- eating to see them joining in the singing of the sweet hymns, and listening to the words that are , spoken." The letter went on to state that Messrs. Naylor, J. Mounfield, and Smethurst were assisting Mr. Skells.nd in seating the Dallam-lane old chapel, which might serve as • a useful Protestant Ragged , School, and appealed for help, either in money or clothing. The work thus unostentatiously begun is already bearing fruit, for the school was cofamenced at the beginning of the year with an attendance of • about 150 children. After the aid of a few friends had been gained in favour of the movement, a meeting was held on the first of this month, at which, on the motion of Mr. Healey, seconded by Mr. Thomas, it was resol- ved that the Committee of the Ragged School, with power to add to their number; be as follows: Rich- ard Dale William Thomas, James Skelland, Emeline Alfred Healey, F. J. Owen, Mary J. Dale, and William H. Butler. It was also decided that Messrs. Osborne and Butler be the secret &ries, that Mr. Skelland be the Superintendent for the next three months, and that Mr. Dale be the trea- surer tor the same period. At the same meeting it was agreed that Miss Millington and Mrs. Dale be authorised to solicit money, clothing, &c. At a se- cond meeting held last Saturday evening, the names of Messrs. Cox, Adams, and Steele, the Misses Brown, and the Misses Dale, Woods, and Maddock were added to the Com- mittee, and various other business was transacted, it being resolved that as soon as should be found practicable, a tea and entertainment should be arranged for, the tea to be for the chil- dren alone, and the public to be, invited to the en- tertainment. Mr. Butler was selected as a fitting person to train the children. At this meeting a Finance Committee, consisting of Messrs:- Owen, Cox, Dale, Skelland, and Thomas, was also formed, and it was decided to name the school "The Warring- ton Ragged Sunday School." From these particulars it will be seen that the undertaking has been entered upon in a thoroughly busines4-like manner, with no half-hearted misgivings, but with the assurance that a work of such moment, so long and so ur- gently needed, must make headway., and increase in usefulness week by week, until its success is as- sured. If the claims that those who have set the work going advance for help are heeded as they should be, hundreds of forlorn children will in fu- ture have something to look forward to each week —a pleasant Sunday afternoon in a warm, comfor- table school, spent with friends who will not des- pise them for their poverty. Hearing that the school was opened on the first Sunday in the year, With about 150 children in atten- dance, one of our reporters was seized with a desire to see for himself how the work was carried on. Ac- cordingly last Sunday afternoon he made his way to the school premises, which have an entrance in Bewsey-street for the visitors, and one in Dallam- lane for the scholars, and received from the Super- intendent a courteous permission to remain. The room' is well suited for the purpose, though possibly as the school gets more and more known, its dimensions may prove too limited. It was warmed by a stove that shed a grateful heat around, and some attempt at Christmas decoratiori had been made. Already abcut a hundred little lads and lasses, of ages ranging from seven to thirteen or fourteen years, were seated on the forms, their faces bright- ened with a new interest. Mr. Skelland and JAL Dale were in chief authority,, and a number of teachers sat here and there among the children, not so much with a view to keep order as to encourage and set them at ease. As yet it had not been found possible to arrange the scholars into classes, or to conduct the school on any pre-arranged plan, and 1 the time was principally occupied in singing and making acquaintance with the ragged visitors. And they were ragged! It was a cheering sight, one to improve one's faith in human nature, to watch the efforts made to bring sunshine into the dark lives of these little ones, but there was something very sad about it, too. Outside the wind was bleak and the streets covered with a cold, slippery slush, and fro & a glance at the bare feet of some of them one's thoughts irresistibly reverted to the hardships they must endure. One brave little fellow, who boasted a fairly decent shirt and a respectable but small pair of pants," was otherwise aatts everything. He was capless, shoeless, and stockingless, and had neither coat nor vest, but yet how cheerful he looked! The comforting heat of the stove was to him a rare treat after -paddlitig through the slush 'and snow, and the singipg ho gloried in. His laird- ships were for the time forgotten. and he was 'haPPY. half-clad, neglected,. may ke but half-fed, yet. happy I You, who worship Sunday, after Sun- day in a well equipped pew in a splendid building, , think of it, Yes, and, do more Lthan think; help these whose lot is so miserable, and surely.you Bliall.have.your reward.. div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF THE EARL OF
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF THE EARL OF
IDDESLEIGII.

It is with great regret that we announce the sudden and almost tragic death of the Earl of Iddes- leigh, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, which occurred on Wednesday afternoon in the Prime Minister's official residence in Downing-street. The noble Earl arrived in London from Pynes on Tues- day evening, in order to fulfil an engagement to speak at the meeting called for Wednesday by the Prince of Wales in support of the proposed Im- perial Institute. He stayed on Tuesday night with Earl Forteicue, at 40, Belgrave Square. At dinner he conversed with his usual animation and, as he was the orly guest, with the least possible reserve or constraint on such topics as presented them- selves. Again, at the family breakfast, between nine and ten, he seemed in good health and spirits. After breakfast, his despatch boxes having arrived from the Foreign Office, he attended to the business demanding his notice. Shortly after- wards he left, and proceeded to the Foreign Office. Sir James Fergusson, Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs, says that Lord Iddesleigh saw him, and spoke for some time very Calmly about leaving Office.' He said, although he thought it better not to accept I any other post at present, he hoped the separation would not be permanent. Mr. H. M. Stanley was waiting to see him about the Emin Bey relief expe- dition. He asked Sir James to see Mr. Stanley, be- I cause he had promised to speak at the Mansion House about the Imperial Institute, but desired him to make an appointment for him at six o'clock. He was looking as well as or better than usual. con- I versed pleasantly about political affairs, and parted i from Sir James n good spirits. The Hon. H. S. Northcote supplied the following particulars I "Lord Iddesleigh, who appeared in his usual health, I went to the Treasury shortly before three o'clock to ; meet Lord Salisbury by appointment. Lord Iddes- ' leigh was received by Mr. Henry Manners, Lord Salisbury not having arrived, and was shown into the waiting-room, where he was left alone. Mr. ; Manners, in the adjoining room, was startled by a cry, and, rushing into the room, found his Lordship in a fainting condition. Raising him in his arms, and finding his efforts to revive him unavailing, he sent for a doctor, who only arrived in time to see his Lordship expire. The cause bf death was syn- cope. Mr. Henry Northcote was summoned at once I from the War Office. He reached the Treasury about half-past three o'clock, and undertook the painful duty of communicating. to Lady Iddesleigh the new's of her husband's sudden death. He left Waterloo for Pynes by the five o'clock train." Dr. Thomas Langston. of 29, Broadway, West- minster, who was the first medical man in atten- dance upon Lord Iddesleigh, has made the following I statement :—" I found Lord Iddesleigh extended at full length on a sofa. Three or four gentlemen were in the room but I do not know who they were. Whether Lord Salisbury was one of the group at the time I entered I cannot say, but I distinctly recol- lect noticing his Lordship passing to and from the room during Lord Iddesleigirs lastmoments, and he waS one of thl small and sorrowing band who gathered around the sofa when, a few minutes after- wards, life was pronounced to be extinct. On ap- proaching the sofa I found Lord Iddesleigh lying ' in a natural position on his back. .I could see al- most from the instant that I appeared upon the scene that the case was hopeless. Everything was sensibly arranged, and it, was evident to me that those around had been prompt in doing all that could be done in such a case. I proposed to apply restoratives, but they were of no avail, and his Lordship passed away peacefully and without a struggle. I should say that the probable cause of death was syncope, in all likelihood occasioned by I some organic disease. The attack which proved' fatal to his Lordship might, in my opinion, have oc- ocurred under the most ordinary circumstances. For instance, it might have been caused by the journey up to town from Exeter. I am aware that Lord Iddesleigh has of late been passing through anxi- ous tithes politically. That might possibly have accelerated his death, but an attack such as that which carried him off was equally possible under the most tranquil conditions, when he had nothing to trouble or worry him." His lordship's family have for a long time been aware that the action of his heart was weak, and might be arrested altogether if he were subjected to sudden excitement. On more than one occasion the fulfilment of their fears has seemed imminent, but latterly the noble Earl has appeared to enjoy better health. His elevation to the House of Lords, a step which brought considerable relief from legis- lative duties, gave him much more leisure,'and a marked improvement in his physical condition was the result. The political occurrences of the last fortnight are believed to have greatly disturbed him, and there can be little doubt that the circum- stances attending his resignation of the Foreign Secretaryship and his subsequent refusal to re-enter the Cabinet brought about a state of mental excite- ment which hastened his death. It had been ar- ranged that 'ie should inove the first resolution at the Mansion House. His non-arrival at the time appointed for the opening of the meeting, half-past three o'clock, caused some little delay, and led to a change in the programme, his lordship's place being assigned to Earl Granville. Lord Granville said he presumed that some accident—probably delay in a train—had interfered with the movements of Lord Iddesleigh, whom he described as a political oppo- nent but an old personal friend, and "one for whose character, both in public and in private, I have the highest possible respect." This expression was re- ceived with hearty cheers. The First Commissioner of Works (Mr. Plunkey) also referred to Lord Iddes- leigh's absence, and said he was sure the meeting would have been glad to hear one who" for so long a period of the present reign has shared in the coun- sels of our Sovereign with so much honour to him- self and so much advantage to the country." The Lord Mayer shortly afterwards announced that a telegram had been received from the Foreign Office stating that Lord Iddesleigh was prevented from attendingthe meeting by sudden indisposition. The Chancellor of the Exchequer added an expression of his regret at the absence of the late Foreign Secre- tary, but during the rest of the proceedings, al- though the news of Lord Iddesleigh's death had reached the meeting, no further reference was made to the subject. Lord Granville and Mr. Goschen had left the hall before the news arrived.

div.head: LORD IDDIiSLEIGH'S CAREER.
div.p: LORD IDDIiSLEIGH'S CAREER.

_ The Right Honourable Sir Stafford Henry North- Cote, eighth baronet and first Earl of Iddesleigh and Viscount St. ewes, G.C.8., P.C. M.A., D.C.L., P.R.S., was born on the 27th of October, 1818. He was the .on of Mr. Henry Stafford Northeote (eldest son of the seventh baronet), by Agnes Mary, the daughter

of Mr. Thomas Cockburn, of Portland-place. Eel was educated at Eton and at Baliol College, Ox- ford. He took his B.A. degree in 1839, and three years later became M.A. In the following year he married Cecilia Frances, daughter of Mr. Thomas Ferrer, of Lincoln's Inn. In the same year Mr. North- cote became private secretary to Mr, Gladstone, who was then President of the Board of Trade, a position which be held for two years. In 1847 he was called the Bar at the Inner Temple, and was then ap- pointed legal secretary to the Board of Trade. On the death of his grandfather, in 1:851, he succeeded to the family honours as eighth baronet. He acted as secretary to the Commissioners of the Great Ex- .hibition (1851), and in acknowledgment of his ser- vices was created a C.B. For several years Sir Staf- ford was engaged with Sir C. E. Trevelyan in an inquiry into the condition of the civil establish- ments of the Crown, and in 1854 they presented a report, which led to the Civil Service being thrown open to public competition. He was first returned to Parliament in 1855, where he represented Dudley in the Conservative interest. Sir Stafford sat for Dud- ley till April, 1857, and from July, 1858, till May, 1866, he was one of the members for Stamford. He was Financial Secretary to the Treasury during the first half of 1859, and on the formation of Lord Derby's third Administration in June, 1866, Sir Stafford was appointed President of the Board of Trade, and sworn in of Privy Council. Three years previously his university had conferred upon him the honorary degree of D.C.L. From March, ' 1867, to December, 1868, he was Secretary of State for India. Sir Stafford was first returned for North Devon in 1866, which constituency he con- tinued to represent until his elevation to the peerage. On the formation of the Conservative Cabinet in 1874 Mr. Disraeli offered him, and he accepted, the post of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. When Mr. Disraeli was created Lord Beaconsfield, Sir Stafford became leader of the the House of Commons. The general election of 1880 resulting in the defeat of the Conservatives, the Government resigned office, and Sir Stafford, after the death of Lord Beaconsfield, became leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons. Just previously he had been made a G.C.B. Mr. Glad- stone having resigned office in June, 1885, Lord Salisbury's first Administration was formed. Sir Stafford, who on the 3rd of July had been created Earl of Iddesleigh and Viscount St. Cyres, occupied the post of First Lord of the Treasury in the new Government, which, after seven months' tenure of office, was succeeded by Mr. Glad- stone's third Cabinet. The last general election having resulted in the overthrow of the Liberal Go- vernment, Lord Salisbury again took office (August, 1886), when Lord Iddesleigh became Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. Consequent on the resignation of Lord Randolph Churchill, Lord Salis- bury decided to take the post of Foreign Secretary, Lord Iddesleigh resigning that office. Lord Iddes- leigh was elected Lord Rector of Edinburgh Univer- sity in 1883, and again in 1886. The deceased peer, who was Lord Lieutenant of Devonshire, was the author of several financial pamphlets, and an Elder Brother of Trinity House. Lord Iddesleigh is sue- 1 ceeded by his son, Viscount St. Eyre, Commissioner of Inland. Revenue, who was born in 1845. EXPRESSIONS OF GRIEF. As the news gradually became known in the poli- tical clubs the excitement was intense, and expres- sions of grief at the untoward event were heard on every hand. The intelligence was at once tele- graphed to the Queen at Osborne and Mr. Gladstone at Hawarden. It was Lord Iddesleigh's intention to proceed to Osborne with the other Ministers on Thursday to hand to her Majesty his seal of office. It was on his return to,Pynes, after being seized with faintness on Tuesday week, that Lord Iddes- leigh first heard, from an unofficial source, that it was proposed that he should leave the Foreign Office. The official communication did not arrive until some hours afterwards. That he felt this step severely there is no question; but he took every opportunity of saying that he was quite sure Lord Salisbury regretted extremely that the result of his conference with Mr. Goschen was inadver- tently made known before it reached the ministers concerned. He did not reglad the state of his health as at all serious, and only as recently as Sat- urday last he asserted himself to be fully equal to the work of the State. At the Carlton Club the prevailing feeling was one of deep regret at the loss the party and the country had sustained; and the peculiarly sensational cir- cumstances under which the tragedy had occurred gave rise to apprehension as to its possible effects upon the Prime Minister, whose health for some time has not been good. At the Liberal clubs the feeling of regret was throughout the evening expressed in earnest terms by politicians of every shade of opinion. The first announcement of the sad event caused an extraor- dinary commotion at the Reform, the Devonshire, and the National Liberal Clubs, it being everywhere taken for granted that it could not fail to have an important bearing upon the future of the Conserva- tive party. In the opinion of Liberals, as expressed at their crabs, Lord Iddesleigit's death is distinctly traceable to the excitement of the last few days, coupled with the grief which he undoubtedly felt at what he regarded as She precipitate close of his public career. Among the innumerable expressions of sympathk which Lord Iddesleigh's death evoked was the fol- lowing from Ilawarden r—"We are sorely grieved at the death of one so eminent, so respected, and so beloved. We must reserve a more particular ex- pression of our feelinge.—(Signed) XATHERINE GLADSTONE." At a meeting of the Conservative electors of the Exchange Division of Liverpool on Wednesday evening, Baron de Worms, M.P., speaking to a reso- lution of condolence with the family of Lord Iddesleigh, said that his Lordship had led his party always with tact, invariably with judgment, and above all things with honour. Ire had been universall3rrepected by all political parties, and his epitaph might well be that he "wore- the white flower of a blameless life It was stated in Liver- pool on Wednesday night, from a BCOUTCe of con- siderable authority, that the Colonial Office was offered to Lord Iddesleigh by the Premier. The same post Wag held under similar circumstances by Lord Granville. LADY IDDESLEIGEI IN LONDON. Lady Iddesleigh, accompanied by Lord St. Cyres and the Rev. John Northcote, left the Pynes, Exe- ter, late on Wednesday night, and travelled by night mail train to Paddington, arriving shortly after' four o'clock on Thursday morning. Lady Iddes- leigh appeared sadly prostrated by her bereave- ment. A representative of the Press Association says : I have had an interview with Dr. Mortimer Gran- vile, who said: I paid two visits to the Countess On Thursday. When I saw her at nine o'clock I found her in the room where the dceased Earl was lying. She had been there in deep grief from the moment she arrived from Exeter at five a.m. Her sorrow was extreme but after some effort I pre- vailed upon her to leave the room, and seek some repose and take a little nutriment. Her efforts for repose have not been successful up to the pre- sent (one p.m.), and I have lust left her. She is bearing up with the greatest fortitude in her ter- rible trouble, the effect of which upon her I' dreaded, specially considering the anguish she must have passed through during her long mght journey from Exeter. I can say she is as weR in health as I could have expected. The Marchionez,s of Salisbury and Lady Gwendo- len Cecil came up to London on Thursday afternoon from Hatfield, to call and offer their condolence to Lady Iddesleigh. MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN, &c. The Queen telegraphed from Osborne on Thurs- day morning to inquire how Lady Iddesleigh has borne her grief, and in what state her ladyship was. A reply was immediately despatched by Dr. Morti- mer Granville, who has seen the Countess, to the effect that she was as well as could be expected under the circumstances. The "Court Circular' says that the Queen re- ceived with sincerest regret the sad intelligence of the death of the Earl of lddesleigh. Her Majesty is deeply concerned at the great foss the country has sustained, and has herself lost a valued and trusted. friend and counsellor, for whom she and her family entertained a true personal regard." Messages of condolence were received on Thurs- day morning from all parts of the country at the London residence of the late Earl, and from an early hour continued to be delivered both by hand and by word of mouth. Lord St. Cyres, who succeeds to the title, is at the house, and the Hon. Henry North- cote, Surveyor-General of Ordnance, is also in town. Throughout Thursday morning there was one constant succession of callers at St. James's.. place, leaving cards and messages of condolence and sympathy with the family of the late Lord Iddesleigh. Ministers, ambassadors, leaders of society, and political men of both parties have vied with each other in showing their respect for the il- lustrious dead, and the high estimation in which he ' was held is further shown by the numberless let- ters and telegrams delivered at the house on Thurs. day morning.

div.head: EXAMINER, SAItIMAY, JANVAItY l5, 1.887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAItIMAY, JANVAItY l5, 1.887.

It is announced that, in consequence of the death of Lord Iddesleigh, her Majesty the Queen, directed the postponement until Friday of the Council at Osborne, which was to have been held on Thurs- day.

FUNERAL ARRANGEMENTS. The funeral of the late Earl of Iddesleigh will take place on Tuesday morning next at the Parish Church of Pynes, Exeter, where the remains will be interred in a vault in the churchyard. The body will be removed on Saturday morning from the town house of the late Earl, 30, St. James s-place, to Pynes. A suggestion has been widely made, but more specially emphasised by members of the dip- lomatic body in London, that a special funeral ser- vice should take place either at 'Westminster Abbey or St. Margaret's Church, Westminster, on Tuesday morning, simultaneously with the ceremony at Pynes Parish Church. Members of every political party have cordially joined in the suggestion,which has been duly placed before the members of the late Earl's family, and it is understood that they have consented to such a course being taken. The proposal has been approved by Dean Bradley, of Westminster Abbey, and Archdeacon Farrail, the vicar of St. Mar- garet's. Westminster, and the necessary arrange- ments are being made. One of the Canons in residence at Westminster Abbey called on Friday morning upon Lord St. Cyres to arrange for the special service which is to be held on Tuesday afternoon at the Abbey. The service, it is understood, will be choral, and the Dean will officiate. A Space will be reserved for the diplomatic corps, personal friends, and dis- tinguished personages, admission to the remainder of the edifice being by ticket. Mr. Bedford, coroner for Westminster, has re- ceived no official intimation respecting the death of Lord Iddesleigh ; and it is not expected now that an inquest will be ordered, particularly asithe de- ceased statesman's medical adviser will certify as to the cause of death. LATEST DETAILS.

The Central N;;;; says rbe-i:e- were again a large I number of callers at St. James-place, on Friday, and I letters and telegrams of condolence poured in throughout the day. All idea of acknowledging such communications separately has necessarily been abandoned, and we have been requested by the late earl's sons to publish the following notifica- tion :—" The family of the late Earl of Iddesleigh desire to express their deep sense of gratitude for the innumerable letters and communications of sympathy which they have received. Their number makes it impossible to acknowledge them sepa- rately, and it is hoped that the late Lord Iddes- leigh's friends will accept this intimation as an explanation of the regrettable absence of indiviitial replies." The state of Lady Iddesleigh's health is begin- I ning to cause considerable anxiety to the members of the family. She insists upon spending many hours daily in the library with the corpse of her late husband, and she is prostrate with grief and almost worn out by want of rest. Her ladyship's health is by no means strong, and she is at present suffering from a bronchial attack, the treatment of which requiries rest and constant care. It is hoped that she may be induced to remain in town at least until Monday, instead of accompanying the remains to Exeter to-day. Nothing has comforted the be- reaved widow more than a touching letter from the Queen, which she has read, and the daily telegrams I of anxious inquiry received from her Majesty. According to the latest arrangements the remains of the late earl will be conveyed to Waterloo sta- tion this (Saturday) morning, and forwarded in a special van by the ordinary eleven train. The principal members of the family and a few personal friends will travel in the same train. The hearse will be full of the flowers, wreaths, and crosses which are pouring in.

ceived both by the classes and the masses in Lon- don. Their stay in the metropolis was an incessant round of acceptance of hospitality. They went out to breitkfast, to luncheon, to dinner, and to supper. Personally, they were very pleasant men, at least the two whom I met on more than. one occasion. One of them spoke excellent French, another al- most faultless English, whilst the third was gene- rally ill. It was startling, on the arrival of the two Delegates, always a little late, to bear that the third was left behind because "he had the fever.' It was, however, un- derstood that the malady was nothing worse tbitn; a cold, and no one feared infection. One advantage we insulars get from the raising of foreign questions . is the knowledge of the proper pronun- ciaticin of strange words. There is, for example, the style of the Bulgarian Parliament, which is commonly pronounced here as it is spelt—So- brange. It is pleasing to he the Bnlgariang call it " Sobrahnee " with the accent, on the middle syll- able.

Loid Randolph Churchill's ppsition may be a I difficklt one; but it is nothing m comparison with that suffered by some other prominent members of the party. Not for the first time in 'recent years have they been diStraught by the necessity of decid- iiig their attitude towards him. He is always calling upon them to take sides, and men like Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, the Baron de Worms, and even larger fry, never quite knoiv-whether it is &der to stand byLord Randolph or to abuse Mm. Looked , at from their point of view, I should certainly be , inclined to keep on good terms with this erratic per- sonage. It is very easy to talk about Lord Randolph having ruined his political prospects by his recent escapade; but I don't think it is likely to be true. He is too indispensable to his party, not rich in striking figures, to be lightly set aside. What the party is without him we have seen since he left the Cabinet. It is also beginning to be seen that he did not do quite such a foolish thing as at first appeared when he chose the ground upon which he elected to leave his colleagues. The taxpayer always has a sneaking affection for a man who insists upon keeping down the estimates. There will presently be an opportunity for a demon- stration within the limits of the party which will determine Lord Randolph's position. About a year ago, when he was a good boy and the rising kope of the Tory party, the new Constitutional Club paid him the highest honour within their power. They already possessed a life-sized portrait of Lord Beaconsfield. They gave a commission to paint one of Lord R. Churchill, to be placed in the new club house side by side with the earlier idol of the party. The portrait will be ready for hanging in the course of a week or two, when occasion will be made to lelicit a kind of popular vote for and against Lord Randolph. The proposal for an Imperial Institute in com- memoration of the Jubilee Year is being pushed with great assiduity. The Prince of Wales having placed himself at the head of the movement, it has become fashionable, and everyone amenable to court influence is, more or less successfully, making be- lieve to be deeply interested in it. Poor Lord Iddes- leigh, anxious at the particular moment to demon- strate his personal loyalty, came up to London and his death, in order to be present at a meeting in furtherance of the scheme. Yesterday East and West were re-united in the good work, meetings:be- ing held simultaneously at St. James's Palace and 1 the Mansion House. Both were attended by many eminent personages, and there is a look of great prosperity about the proposal. But it is really a very hollow affair, and will have to be nursed assi- duously if it is to be carried through the delicate period of infancy. Somehow or other the masses do , not take to it, and the classes are not accustomed to I carry the weight of such a prodigious enterprise. The hostile feeling is doubtless due to prejudice. But there i is, and it threatens to blight the project. A very interesting controversy has been raised by the assertion, dug out of some parish ma- gazine, that the late Archdeacon Allen was the pro- totype of Major Dobbin. Those who knew the late Archdeacon in the flesh, and never before thought , he was like Major Dobbin, cannot fail to see the re- semblance the moment the suggestion is made. A big, loosely-made, high-shouldered man, with Smooth face always ready to wrinkle in a kindly , smile, slouching walk, and simple frank manners. I If the Archdeacon did not really it for the immor- tal portrait he well might have done.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

ENTERTAINMENT AT Kir ostay.-.The annual parochial tea party was held on Tuesday evening, in the girls' school- room, when, notwithstanding the unfavourable weather, the tables were well attended. Afterwards a concert was held in the larger schoolroom, in which the following ladies and gentlemen took part :—Master G. Steele (pianoforte over- ture), Miss K. Rigby, of Frodshana ; Miss Hopkins, Miss Jackson, Mr. Jackson. Mr. C. E. Hitchen, and Mr. C. Riley, of Frodsham. The Vicar of Frodsham (Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A.) gavejwo songs, the first of which elicited a well. deserved encore. The comic portion of the programme was well sustained by Mr. E. J. Steward. The entertain- ment was brought to a close by the singing of the .National , Anthem.

SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' CONFERENCE.—OR Saturday afternoon the teachers and officers of the I'rimitive Meth,- dist Sunday Schools of Preston Brook station were invited to meet the secretary of the Connexions! Union, the Rev. T. Whittaker, of Leeds, at Frodsham, to discuss certain phases of Sunday school work. The very severe weather militated against a large attendance. There were present the Rev. J. Causland (Runcoin), superintendent of the station; Rev. T. Lagan, Frodsham ; Messrs. Riley, W. Jones, J. Hough, W. Booth, J.Sayles (Runcorn), dm. From a. report furnished by the Rev. T. Whittaker, it appears that the Primitive Methodists have 3,753 Sunday schools, 67 of which were opened last year, and of the total number 2,933 are affiliated with the Union. The number of teachers (gratuitous) is 58.121; and of scholars 386,570, showing an increase for the year of 5,755. The number of scholars who are members of society is 28,243; while 99,679 are members of the Bands of Hope, the pledge of which is the threefold one of abstention from intoxicating drinks, to- bacco, and snuff. The total income of the schools for the year was £56,686 6s 9d, being £155 in advance of the pre- ceding year. Indeed, progress marks each department. Conversations then ensued on the questions—" How can we best secure an efficient supply of female teachers 2" and s' What means could most effectually be employed to in- terest our members and congregations generally in Sunday school work 2" Other topics were also introduced and dis- cussed, and a profitable afternoon was spent. On Sunday, Mr:Whittaker visited the school at Frodsham. and addressed the scholars and teachers. He also preached in the chapel afternoon and evening, emphasizing the duty and import- ance of earnest attention to Sunday school work on the part of the churches.

VISITS TO THE. QUEEN. The Prime Minister, who was looking much distressed. arrived at Portsea from London about noon on Thursday, and crossed to East C,wes. Lord Salisbury then drove in one of the Royal carriages to Osborne, on a visit to the Queen. His lordship returned to London from Osborne shortly before six o'clock on Friday evening. Lord Cranbrook, Mr. Goschen, Mr. Smith, 114 r. Stanhope and Sir Henry liollawl left Victoria Terminus (London) at halipast nine on Friday morning for Portsmouth, on their way to Osborne, to attend a meeting of the Privy Council, toe the transference of the seals. The seals of the late Lord iddealeigh and Lord Randolph Churchill were conveyed by Mr. Lennox Peel.
The Central News save: At Osborne Lord Salisbury would join his colleagues, and the whole 0 the Ministers would kiss hands on their new appointments.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORURSPORDENT.I 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The present aspect of the Stock Exchange is best de- scribed as one of expectancy, an expectancy, too, that is possible of realization. Although the markets show little effect of the speech of Prince Bismarck, there is little doubt but that the war cloud is the one overshadowing doubt which prevents the markets from going up almost with a bound. The early part of the week was almost entirely occupied with the settlement, which was in every respect more satisfactory than the last. There were no anticipations of heavy failures, money was easier ; in fact, every element which combined to make last settlement so much dreaded was abaent at the settlement just closed. Prices generally were stronger, Home Rails in particular showing au advance. At the previous settlement the making up prices of Home Rails were depressed, owing to heavy sales by weak holders. The following is sufficient to show the improved tone :—Great Northern : At making up prices this settlement was 107 i, previous settlement 108; London and North-Western, pre- ' sent,settlement 184, last, 161 i ; Brighton A's, present sot. i Cement 119, last 114. These examples are sufficient te show the improved tone of the market, and since these ! prices were made, the market all round improved, land the latest prices are indicative of firmness. The declaration of the half yearly dividends of the leading railways have not been disappointing, and have come up to expectations. Metropolitan, Brighton, and South-Eastern have declared dividends of 4; Brightbn Ordinary 8, A's 41, and the last-named company 71. With improved trade there can be little doubt that prices will go !higher, and with indications of such improvement as in the increased traffic returns of North British there is only one element required, and that is confidence in the maintenance of peace and absence of political disturbance. The absence of all companies during the past few weeks is an indication that promoters are pretty correct guages of the fitness of 1 things financial. The time, however, is fast approach- ing when if:treaters will be overwhelmed with the number, and discrimination is necessary in selectiag the , good from the bad. That there are some good goes without saying, as likewise that there will be some very bad. It is to joint stock enterprise that most of the progress, commer- cially, during the past few years is owing, at the sametime there is much in the Joint Stock Companies' Acts that re- quires amendment,and country investors particularly require protection, which, even if existing, to incur the necessary expense they could not always insure obtaining in the pre- sent unsatisfactory state of the Companies' Acts, and I would conclude by advising intending investors always to satisfy themselves on the nature of the contracts,as it is upon these that the whole success tr failure of the com- pany hangs.

div.head: 0 Ult LONDONITETTE
div.p: 0 Ult LONDONITETTE

• LONDON, THURSDAY. The news of the death of Lord Iddesleigh apread with remarkable rapidity. It was somewhere about a quarter to three when he fell dead in the ante- room adjoining that in. which Lord Salisbury sat, and by half-past four the boys were shouting the news up and down the astonished Strand. -.3ut nearly an hour earlier the news was beginning tobe whispered through the Reform, Club, where it had corae from the Foreign Office. It was so sudden, so terrible, and so tragic that in the case of other men there would have been indisposition to believe it. But those who had personal acquaintance with Lord Iddesleigh knew that nothing was more p bable. For years he has suffered from heart dis- ease, the warning symptoms of• which have flue-, tuated with political crises. The first time the fact was made known outside the family circle was dur- ing the height of the revolt of the Fourth Party, when Lord Randolph Churchill and Sir Henry Wolff goading at him every night in the House of Com- mons, Sir Stafford Northcote was obliged, after a brief spasmodic effort, to retire into the back- ground. I can see him as it were but yesterday sitting on the front Opposition bench with' head bowed down and hands thrust up either sleeve, whilst on the corner bench below the gangway stands Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, with face turned full upon his nominal chief and outstretched forefingernvockingly pointed at him; behind Lord Randolph, with hat tilted over his forehead, arms folded, sits Sir Henry Wolff on the extreme-edge of the bench., so that he may. get a better view of the evident pain of the victim. • The work has been finished now, and the chivalrous, unselfish, kindly gentleman is beyond the reach of personal malevolence or political jealousy. Of those left behind, so'one is more sin- cerely to be pitied than Lord Salsbury. Through all his public life Lord Iddesleigh has been 'a close companion. He has known him better than most men, and must,, therefore, have liked him more. Yet, if Lord Salisbury had had more firmness, and had stood with more determination, between his old friend and those who were hunting him to death, Lord Iddesleigh would have been alive to- day. No one questions that his sudden and tragic death was the immediate result of the ea-oirement, anxiety, and personal humiliation to which he has I been subjected during the past ton days. To-day, the Round Table Conference meets, and unless—what is not impossible—insuperable points of 'difference present themselves at the opening it will sit again to-morrow. It may be interesting for comparison with the accomplished'results to state on the threshold of the meeting that it is not regardcd with high hope by those most intimately acquainted with its conditions and chances. Practically, every- thing will depend upon Mr. Chamberlain.. if he is really desirous of returning ta the Liberal fold, a bridge as handsome-and convenient as possible will be built for him. But it is he that will have to cross the bridge, and not Mr. Gladstone and the great majority of the Liberal party. If Mr. Chamber- jam's spokesmen in the Birmingham press are to be believed he will not budge an inch from the position he has taken up. But that is, on the face. of it, absurd. If he does not mean te give in what sifts his object in proposing the Conference and in now entenng upon it? Mr. Labouchere has a very ready explanation. He says that "Joe," as he familiarly styles the former object of his regal, has suggested the Conference with the simple ',ob- ject of showing himself accessible and amenable. If nothing comes of it he can say, "Look what a good boy am I I have tried every means to lying about the reunion of the Liberal party, but have been foiled by the criminal obstinacy of Mr. Glad- stone and his friends." Mr. John Morley takes a more hopeful view of Mr. Chamberlain's disposi- tion; but Mr. Morley is not so sanguine. of the result. The Visit of the Bulgarian Delegates was, as far as it went, a great success. They, of course, gained nothing by their interviews With Lord Spencer or Lord Iddesleigh. But they were very kindly re-

JEwisll bIkRRIAGE AT WIDNES.

A marriage h which considerable interest was manifested wit); solemnised at Widnes on Thursday afternoon. It was the union of Miss Janie Sophia CfacM yvho resided with her brother, Mr. S. S. Claff, furnitu."e dealer, Ann-street West, and Mr. Mendel Blank, of Manchester, a member of the firm of Messrs.. elate` and Co., furni- ture dealers, and it was the firsAt marrik,,,ge that had taken place in the town accordirq to the custom of the Jews, the happy couple being' a the Hebrew faith. There being no synagogue in the town, the ceremony took place in the dining-Isom of the Mersey Hotel, and there were a large number of friends, Jewish and Christian, present. The usual preliminaries imposed by the Hebrew' faith had been observed by the "happy couple," including fasting from the previous evening, and they had not enjoyed each other's society alone for twen- ty-four hours. The celebrant was the Rev. 8. Alexander, of Cheetham Hill Great Spa, gue, Manchester, and Mr. H. Harris, secretag, ma registrar of the synagogue, was present in ,hos official capacity. Whilst the room was occupied only by males, the reverend gentleman, the bride- groom, and a person who appeared to fulfil the offices of church clerk, retired into a corner of the room, and went through a service apparently for the sole benefit of the bridegroom. The prayers w3re chanted. At the conclusion of the service, the shoulders of the bridegroom were enveloped in a white silken robe, with a deep blue border, and a crimson Canopy was erected in the centre of the room. Under this the priest. and bridegroom took positions, and then ,the bride; who was tastefully attired in a dress of heliotrope silk, and from whose head debended along white veil, entered the room attended by a numerous train of ladies. She proceeded to the right hand of the bridegroom; Mrs. S. Cleft and Mrs. Blank also tak- ing positions under the canopy. The bridesmaids were Miss Rosie Gwdman 'and Miss Lizzie Blank. The reverend gentleman tben chanted from a manu- script enclosed in a frame, and concluded by read- ing the covenant entered into by the pair. During the proceedings both bride and bridegroom drank twice from a silver goblet, and the seal of marriage was consummated by the bridegroom crashing a piece of glass under the heel of his right foot, signi- fying that until those pieces were again welded together, the covenant would be inviolate. About 60 guests afterwards sat down to dinner, and at six o'clock a ball was held.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
-. A monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Court House, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon; Mr. E. Greenall presided, and there was a large atten- dance of members.

A COMPLAINT PROM WESTON POINT. A letter was read complaining of the shocking condition of the South-road at Weston Point, and stating that all the owners of property adjoining the road ex,cept one were wil- ling to contribute their share towards repairing the road. The Board were asked if they could not put pressure on this ratepayer. —The CHAIRMAN said the Board had nothing to de with the road.—Mr. AARON asked if the Board had no power to compel the owners to put the road into proper re. pair.—The CHAIRMAN: Certainly not.—Mr. AARON said it was only right that the property owners should put the road into repair, and it was a pity there was no law to com- pel them to do eo.—The matter then dropped. A THREATENED APPEAL. A letter, was read from Mr. Cox complaining of the state of the road leading from Dutton Lodge to Sutton Weaver, and stating that if nothing were done be would appeal to the Authority in London.—A Member of the Beard said that be thought the road referred to was in a better condition just now than it had ever been in before and another Mem- ber remarked that Mr. Cox might complain to the Authority if he liked, but there was no reason why he should he better served than anybody else.—The subject then dropped. TIP EITCROACHMENT AT APPLETON THORN'. The CHAIRMAN referred to the recent encroachment on the highway at Appleton Thorn through the building of the new church there, and denied that he had ever expressed himself satisfied with the way in which the encroachment had been made, but on the contrary, he bad told the Sur- veyor distinctly that it was a matter. entirely for the High- way Board. This difficulty had come, about entirely through the neglect and carelessness of the Surveyor. He (the chairman) had told him he wee not fit to be the surveyor, and be repeated it. Although the church had been building since January and February last, the Sur- veyor had never reported the matter to them, and now they were landed in a mess; it was perfectly disgraceful the way the Surveyor had treated them, for If'it had not been for two members of that Board they would never have heard a word about it. The Chairman then read the report of the committee appointed to deal with the matter, which re- commended that on, Mr. Warburton placing the watt as shown on the plan presented to them the Board should take no further steps in the matter. He also moved the adop- tion of,the report.—Mr. W. LONG seconded the propoaal, and endorstd the remarks of the Chairman with regard to the awkward position the Hoard bad been placed in. They felt that Mr. Warburton had hid a certain encouragement given to him in that matter which would not have met with the consent of the Board. The committee found that certain promises had in a measure been made to Mr. War- burton, and even a letter had 6een submitted to him by the Surveyor which he (Mr. Long understood the Chairman ha& recommended the Surveyor not to send.—The CHAramAN That is so.—Mr. Lernia,said they had been dismayed to find that that letter bad been submitted to Mr. Warburton, showing that it was the Surveyor's opinion that the en. croachment was really of no copseauence.—Sir GILBERT' GRRRNALL thought that if pi ins had been submitted in the first instance by the builder, that difficulty would not have arisen. (Hear, bear.)—The CHAIRMAN maintained that the whole fault lay with their Surveyor.—The SURVEYOR pointed out that the first intimation he had of the encroach- ment was on the23rd October, two days before he submitted a plan to the Chairman.—The report of the committee was I then adopted.

ALTERATIONS AT WILDEBSPOOL. Mr. Downs, on behalf of Messrs. Greenell, Whitley, Co., submitted plans of proposed alterations to the road at Wilderspool, the object being to provide a saferand bentr entrance for drays, dze., to the brewery. After some con- sideration of the plans it seemed to be the unanimous opinion of the Board that the proposed alterations would be a great improvement upon present arrangements, and they were ultimately with some slight amendments sanctioned. This was the principal business before the meeting.

ST. JAMES'S CHURCH, LATCH FORD. ANNUAL TEA PARTY AND ENTER,TAINMENT. The annual parochial tea party and entertain- ment in connection with St. James' Church were held on Monday evening, in the new schools, Latch- ford. The tea was served in the large school-room, there being about 300 persons present . The follow- ing is a list of the• ladies and gentlemen who, gave either trays or money :—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P. (2) ; Mesdames Slater, J. White, H. N. Mugh- ton, J. Warburton. Harrison, R. Greenall, Don, J. Bolton, Taylor, Radnall, F. Pierpoint, Venn, Hutchinson, Francomb, Pye, Sherratt, Pictoni Ayl- ward, Holliwell, Bowes, Cook, Warrall, Cooper, Mill- wood, Pilling, Tawranac, Green, Wright, Harvey, F. Wright,. Woods, McGowan, Buertoni Hitchmough, Young, Henry, Hallwood, Lee, Wilson,. Jones, Brown, 8., C. Cooper, and Seed; the Misses H. Har- vey, Smith, Parry, Smith, and Hodson; and Messrs. Pearce, Rawson and Co., Riley, J. Davies, J. Edles- ten and Co., Wright (Stockton Heath), Hales, Adams, Price, Walton, Wynne Jones, Marson, C. Burgess, Messrs. Milling- and Co., and Messrs. Tinsley. Afterwards the room was cleared and the entertainment given, Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., pre- siding. In the course of the evening several short addresses were given. Sir GILBERT GREENALL said be was pleased and thank- ful that the school belonged to the poor people of that parish'. Ha was also thankful that the school bad been paid far, and that there was not one shilling owing upon it- (Applause.) The Bev. F. SLATER said that while during the past yea:, they had had those won2erful schools completed and paid for they had had to give up almost as ajoonsequence a little bit of work which many of them held very dear, and that was their mission house. At the time the mission house was opened they had no sahool like that, but now they had got that school with numberless classrooms, and they had better accommodation than ever they had in the old minion house, Mere than that, the day nursery was net properly used. He eapposed that mothers preferred tO nurse their own babies, at any rate they did not send them to tha day nursery in sufficient numbers to make it worth while, keep. log it on. They had, therefore. moved out of thelarge house into a small one in St. Margaret's-lane, about a hun- dred, yards away. Every parish had its difficulties, and they had theirs. In a parish like that, with a largo number of poor people, and hardly anyone very well to do, one of the great diffisulties to be contended with was the need of raising money. Not having is large endowment that diffi- culty was to be faced continually, and he was happy and proud to think that they bad had f Hands outside their own parish who had tendered them again and again such help as very few parishes in the country could boast of. (Hear, hear.) When they stood in that building, which had coot £3,500% and thought that it had been built in poor little LatchlOrd, they had much to be thankful for. (Hear, hear.) There was one thing he should like to mention, and that was that he should very much like to see their church before neat Easter put In a worthier condition. It wanted, what all their houses wanted now and then to be cleaned and painted, and in the jubilee year they should see if they could not do something in that direction in their own parish. (Applause.) Mr. Jonx Warn also gave a abort address in the course of the evening. He referred to the fact, as shown in "St. James' Quarterly Magazine," that the churchwardens were is debt. lie saw that the debt amounted to 010, but he had

heard that day that one half of that amount had been Pt raised by Mr. John Tinsley and Mr. W. Sharp, and be had ' no doubt that the rest of it would be forthcomiog. But 135 was desirous that when the church was got out of debt it should beltept ovt of debt. (Hear, hear.) The endowment of that church was very email, the actual endowment been only £B5 a year and the vicar having given up the PeW: rents in order that the seats might be free to the poorer pa' ishioners, he had done away with the most important part of his income. It was only right that Mr. Slater should be 11 loser by this transattion, but he (Mr. White) was afro he had been a loser, because the offertory, of which tile vicar received a part, was not whatlit should be. no °ft tory for the year, excluding the special offertories, was 00., /MO, and that he (Mr. White) thought was not sufgcient' , The parish was not so poor but that more might be done in' side the parish. He had heard the other day of a church e't which there was a congregation one morning consisting ofl peer of the realm, two squires of the neighbourhood, the' families and households, and numerous well-to-do farteer!(, net yet the whole of the mernixg's offertory only amolint' fts 60. (Laughter.) After that they might think tba'„, St Jamees, with its offertory a 503 or 60s of a Soodayde did.well in comparison; but if there were ZO people-4D there ought totes that number of Church people in that, parish—mho would give 6d per wesk,• they would raisea.l that'iras required. He made these remarks bciuse be ' not wish them to lose such a goo 3 vicar an" Mr. Sißte'' (Applause.) of' In the course of the evening an ex:allent programme „„ music was rendered the items, Includicg a duet by- ' Grounds and Mika Ninon; song, M. J. White; doe," Rae'. T. P. and Mrs. Williamson ; song, lii'. Grounds; n°.l;l' Mr. F. Like; song, Mrs. Williamson; comic song, Bowes. Alderman Davies also caused a great deal ° amusement by the relating of two stories, cmd the perfornr sneer, of the Latchford String Band, under the conductor: k ship of the Rev. F. Slater, were prolific of entertainmen,, Mr. Walter Roselle and his." tar:lily of fungy folks" °ft i likewise present, and gave an exceedingly cNver Yeovil(' guild performance. A vote of thanks was moved to Sir Gilbert Greenal for presiding by Councillor Hutchinson, one of the-church Or.;. dens, and this having been heartily accorded, SirGilbert.,l„, responding, intimated amidst applause his intention to WI; £5O towards the expense of cleaning and beautifYirlit it church. It was mentioned by the Rev. F. Slater that ,n • Iwas estimated the cost of this work would be between and £6O, and Alderman Davies thereupon off wed to deft°, the balance, an offer which was cordially accepted. log The proceedings were brought to a•close by the saig of the national anthem.
